title: Applied Statistics
text:
Preface
This book is not written for statisticians. It is for everyone else that uses statistics in their work: ecologists, medical researchers, psychologists, and so on. You need some overview of what methods exist and when to use them. You probably don’t have time (or interest) to start with the mathematical foundations and build your knowledge from the ground up. That is why this book takes a different approach, rooted in application.

title: Probability Distributions
text:
Functions describing the probability of different outcomes of random events.

Just because something is random does not mean every outcome is equally likely. Probability distributions describe how likely each possible outcome of a random event is.
To get started, familiarize yourself with these three probability distributions:

The  normal distribution (continuous processes with a central tendency)
The  Poisson distribution (counts)
The  binomial distribution (ratios, proportions, binary data)

The video below introduces these and provides some intuition.

 Open video in a new tab
There are many other useful probability distributions which we will learn about as we progress, but these three form the starting point for many analyses.
The last chapter in this section introduces  hypothesis testing.






TipWhat level of detail do I need for the exam?





If you are using this book in the context of one of my courses, please note the following:

You do not need to master every detail in this section. The goal is a working understanding you can build on.
Aim to finish this section within a day. We will revisit the concepts extensively in the following sections.
On the exam, probability distributions only come up in the context of regression analysis, so focus your efforts on those sections.

title: Normal Distribution
text:
Properties
A continuous, symmetric probability distribution that is bell-shaped.
The normal distribution (also: Gaussian distribution) is used to model continuous processes where most values are close to the mean, deviations in either direction are equally likely, and further deviations are increasingly less likely. It is extremely common in statistics, not because it is particularly realistic, but because it is convenient to work with mathematically and often a reasonable approximation.

title: Normal Distribution
text:
Probability density functionCumulative distribution functionQuantile function



What is the height of the curve at a given point?








Figure 1: Probability density of a standard normal distribution (\(\mu = 0\), \(\sigma^2 = 1\)).






Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
  \tag{1}\label{dnorm}
  \mathcal{N}(\mu, \, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}} e ^ {- \frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}
\end{align}\]


Code:


RPython



dnorm(x, mean, sd)




from scipy.stats import norm
norm.pdf(x, loc, scale)

Note: loc refers to the mean, scale to the standard deviation.











NoteSymbols






\(\mathcal{N}\): A normal distribution
\(\mu\): The mean of the distribution
\(\sigma^2\): The variance of the distribution
\(\pi\): The constant 3.141593… (why?)
\(e\): The constant 2.718282… (why?)
\(x\): The value of a given observation










TipExplanation





The normal distribution is a continuous probability distribution. This has an important implication: The \(y\)-axis in Figure 1 shows probability density, not probability. For an explanation, please refer to the video. If you actually want to calculate probabilities, you have to calculate the surface area under the curve, which can be done with the cumulative distribution function.
The total area under the curve of a probability distribution always equals \(1\).
Imagine a rectangular probability distribution (also called a uniform distribution):








Figure 2: Uniform distribution on \(a = 0.5\), \(b = 1\).





The probability density goes all the way to \(2\), but since there is only a non-zero probability density between \(0.5\) and \(1\), the surface area under the curve still sums up to a total probability of \(2 \times 0.5 = 1\).
The standard normal distribution refers to a normal distribution with \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma^2 = 1\).









CautionExamples






RPython


The top of the curve (\(x = 0\)) in Figure 1 has a height of:

dnorm(x = 0, mean = 0, sd = 1)

[1] 0.3989423


At \(x = 2\), the curve has a height of:

dnorm(2, 0, 1)

[1] 0.05399097


Using the following code, you can plot a normal distribution with \(\mu = 1\) and \(\sigma^2 = 0.09\):

x <- seq(0, 2, 0.01)
y <- dnorm(x, 1, 0.3)
plot(x, y, type = "l")












The top of the curve (\(x = 0\)) in Figure 1 has a height of:

from scipy.stats import norm
y = norm.pdf(x = 0, loc = 0, scale = 1)
print(y)

0.3989422804014327


At \(x = 2\), the curve has a height of:

y = norm.pdf(2, 0, 1)
print(y)

0.05399096651318806


Using the following code, you can plot a normal distribution with \(\mu = 1\) and \(\sigma^2 = 0.09\):

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.arange(0, 2, 0.01)
y = norm.pdf(x, loc = 1, scale = 0.3)
plt.plot(x, y)
plt.show()


















What is the probability (surface area) up till a given point \(z\)?








Figure 3: Cumulative distribution function of a standard normal (\(\mu = 0\), \(\sigma^2 = 1\)).






Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
  \tag{2}\label{pnorm}
  \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \int_{-\infty}^z e^{- \frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \sigma^2}} \mathrm{d}x
\end{align}\]


Code:


RPython



pnorm(z, mean, sd)




from scipy.stats import norm
norm.cdf(z, loc, scale)

Note: loc refers to the mean, scale to the standard deviation.











NoteSymbols






\(\pi\): The constant 3.141593… (why?)
\(\sigma^2\): The variance of the distribution
\(\int_{-\infty}^z \dots \mathrm{d}x\): The integral (surface area) from \(-\infty\) to \(z\)
\(e\): The constant 2.718282… (why?)
\(\mu\): The mean of the distribution
\(x\): The value of a given observation










TipExplanation





The cumulative distribution function (CDF) is the integral of the probability density function up till a given point \(z\). It can be used to calculate the probability of an observation being less than a certain value. To obtain the opposite—the chance of an observation being equal to or greater than a certain value, simply use \(1\) minus the CDF. Finally, to compute the chance of being within a certain range, you can subtract the CDF of the smaller value, from the CDF of the larger value (see the examples below).
Around 95% of observations fall within two standard deviations of the mean. This holds for any normal distribution, so you can check it with the standard normal, which is what the function uses if you leave out the mean and standard deviation:

RPython



pnorm(2) - pnorm(-2)

[1] 0.9544997





from scipy.stats import norm
p = norm.cdf(2) - norm.cdf(-2)
print(p)

0.9544997361036416














CautionExamples






RPython


If adult males in The Netherlands are \(1.838\) m on average, with a standard deviation of \(7\) cm, the chance of being 2 meters or taller is:

1 - pnorm(2, 1.838, 0.07)

[1] 0.01032603


To compute the probability of a range, just subtract the smaller value from the greater:

# Probability of being within 5 cm from the mean
pnorm(1.888, 1.838, 0.07) - pnorm(1.788, 1.838, 0.07)

[1] 0.5249495




Visual interpretation











The probability of a value of \(z \leq -1.5\) in Figure 3 is given by:

pnorm(-1.5, mean = 0, sd = 1)

[1] 0.0668072




If adult males in The Netherlands are \(1.838\) m on average, with a standard deviation of \(7\) cm, the chance of being 2 meters or taller is:

from scipy.stats import norm
p = 1 - norm.cdf(2, 1.838, 0.07)
print(p)

0.010326027446208808


To compute the probability of a range, just subtract the smaller value from the greater:

# Probability of being within 5 cm from the mean
p = norm.cdf(1.888, 1.838, 0.07) - norm.cdf(1.788, 1.838, 0.07)
print(p)

0.5249494759460464




Visual interpretation











The probability of a value of \(z \leq -1.5\) in Figure 3 is given by:

p = norm.cdf(-1.5, loc = 0, scale = 1)
print(p)

0.06680720126885807












Up till what point does the surface area equal a given probability \(p\)?








Figure 4: Quantile function of a standard normal distribution (\(\mu = 0\), \(\sigma^2 = 1\)).






Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
  \tag{3}\label{qnorm}
  \mu +  \sqrt{2\sigma^2} \cdot \mathrm{erf}^{-1}(2p - 1)
\end{align}\]


Code:


RPython



qnorm(p, mean, sd)




from scipy.stats import norm
norm.ppf(probability, loc, scale)

Note: loc refers to the mean, scale to the standard deviation.











NoteSymbols






\(\mu\): The mean of the distribution
\(\sigma^2\): The variance of the distribution
\(\mathrm{erf}^{-1}\): The inverse error function, which has no closed form, but can be approximated numerically










TipExplanation





The quantile function is the inverse of the cumulative distribution function. It tells you up till what point the probability equals \(p\). To obtain the opposite—the point after which the probability equals a certain value, simply compute the quantile of \(1\) minus the probability (see the examples below).









CautionExamples






RPython


How tall (at least) are the tallest 5% of adult males in The Netherlands?(Assuming a normal distribution with \(\mu = 1.838\), \(\sigma = 0.07\))

qnorm(0.95, 1.838, 0.07)

[1] 1.95314


Within which heights are 95% of adult males in The Netherlands?

qnorm(c(0.025, 0.975), 1.838, 0.07)

[1] 1.700803 1.975197




How tall (at least) are the tallest 5% of adult males in The Netherlands?(Assuming a normal distribution with \(\mu = 1.838\), \(\sigma = 0.07\))

from scipy.stats import norm
y = norm.ppf(0.95, 1.838, 0.07)
print(y)

1.953139753886603


Within which heights are 95% of adult males in The Netherlands?

y = norm.ppf([0.025, 0.975], 1.838, 0.07)
print(y)

[1.70080252 1.97519748]

title: Normal Distribution
text:
Quiz

Question 1Answer


If adult female height in The Netherlands can be reasonably approximated by a normal distribution with \(\mu = 1.704\) m and \(\sigma = 7\) cm, what percentage is taller than \(1.80\) m?






NoteHint





First, convert both to the same unit: \(\mu = 1.704\) m, \(\sigma = 0.07\) m.(Converting both to cm works as well.)
Then, use the code under Examples in the probability density function tab to plot the distribution. This is the best way to get a feel for it.









Now you can already see from the figure that the answer must be some small number, as \(1.8\) is already well into the tails.
The question can be answered with the cumulative distribution function.









CautionTry it in browser






Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.





Use \(1\) minus the cumulative distribution function to find the probability in the right tail of the distribution.

RPython



1 - pnorm(1.8, 1.704, 0.07)

[1] 0.0851207





from scipy.stats import norm
p = 1 - norm.cdf(1.8, 1.704, 0.07)
print(p)

0.0851206979548067





About \(8.5\%\) is taller than \(1.8\) m.













Question 2Answer


Suppose the beak length of medium ground finches (Geospiza fortis) can be reasonably approximated using a normal distribution with a mean of 11.0 mm with a standard deviation of 0.5 mm. Within what range do you expect 90% to fall?





Example of a medium ground finch.










NoteHint





Use the code under Examples in the probability density function tab to plot the probability distribution. This is the best way to get a feel for it.









Now you can already see what would be a plausible answer… perhaps around 10–12 mm?
The question can be answered with the quantile function.









CautionTry it in browser






Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.





Use the quantile function from \(5\%\) to \(95\%\) to find the middle \(90\%\):

RPython



qnorm(c(0.05, 0.95), 11, 0.5)

[1] 10.17757 11.82243





from scipy.stats import norm
y = norm.ppf([0.05, 0.95], 11, 0.5)
print(y)

[10.17757319 11.82242681]





\(90\%\) of beak lengths are expected to be within \(10.2\) and \(11.8\) mm.

title: Poisson Distribution
text:
Properties
A discrete, non-negative probability distribution that can be right skewed.
The Poisson distribution is the number of events happening in a fixed amount of time. It is used to model counts. If events are truly independent and occur at a fixed rate, then the Poisson distribution is not an approximation, but the probability distribution of counts.
In reality, counts are often not completely independent: Birds do not arrive randomly, independently in a park, but actually tend to group together. For this reason, analyses based on a Poisson distribution should include some assessment of whether the chosen distribution is realistic. These assessments will be introduced once we get to the topic of GLM.

title: Poisson Distribution
text:
Probability mass functionCumulative distribution functionQuantile function



What is the probability of a given count \(k\)?








Figure 1: Probability mass function of a Poisson distribution with \(\lambda  = 3\).






Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
  \tag{1}\label{dpois}
  \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}
\end{align}\]


Code:


RPython



dpois(k, lambda)




from scipy.stats import poisson
poisson.pmf(k, mu)

Note: mu refers to the mean (\(\lambda\)).











NoteSymbols






\(\lambda\): The rate parameter, representing both mean and variance
\(e\): The constant 2.718282… (why?)
\(k\): The value of a given count
\(!\): Factorial (e.g., \(3! = 3 \times 2 \times 1\))










TipExplanation





The Poisson distribution is a discrete probability distribution. There are only certain possible values for the outcome, like \(0, 1, 2, \dots\), but not \(1.5\) or \(2.01\). Hence, you can directly read probabilities off the \(y\)-axis in Figure 1.
The correct term for a probability function of a discrete distribution is a probability mass function, though it is common in literature to see people call both discrete and continuous versions a probability density function.
Note that while it looks like the probability goes to zero after \(k = 10\) in Figure 1, it never exactly reaches zero. The probability is just too small to be visible in the figure.
Counts cannot be negative. If lambda is close to zero, the probability on the left side of the distribution gets pressed up into the side. If you increase lambda, you move further away from zero, so this skew becomes less apparent:








Figure 2: Increasing \(\lambda\) results in a more symmetric distribution.














CautionExample






RPython


The probability of \(k = 4\) in Figure 1 is:

dpois(4, lambda = 3)

[1] 0.1680314


Using the following code, you can plot the probability mass function of Poisson distribution with \(\lambda = 2\):

x <- 0:20
y <- dpois(x, 2)
plot(y ~ x, type = "h", lwd = 4, lend = 1, las = 1)










The probability of \(k = 4\) in Figure 1 is:

from scipy.stats import poisson
y = poisson.pmf(4, mu = 3)
print(y)

0.16803135574154085


Using the following code, you can plot the probability mass function of Poisson distribution with \(\lambda = 2\):

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import poisson
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.arange(0, 21)
y = poisson.pmf(x, 2)
plt.bar(x, y);
plt.show()


















What is the probability up till a given point \(k\)?








Figure 3: Cumulative distribution function of a Poisson distribution with \(\lambda = 3\).






Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
  \tag{2}\label{ppois}
  \sum_{i = 0}^k \frac{\lambda^i e^{-\lambda}}{i!}
\end{align}\]


Code:


RPython



ppois(k, lambda)




from scipy.stats import poisson
poisson.cdf(k, mu)

Note: mu refers to the rate \(\lambda\).











NoteSymbols






\(\lambda\): The rate parameter, representing both mean and variance
\(e\): The constant 2.718282… (why?)
\(k\): The value of a given count
\(!\): Factorial (e.g., \(3! = 3 \times 2 \times 1\))
\(\sum\): Summation (compute for \(0, 1, \dots, k\) and add all results)










TipExplanation





The cumulative distribution function (CDF) is the sum of the probability mass function up till a given point \(k\). It can be used to calculate the probability of a count being no greater than a certain value. To obtain the opposite—the chance of an observation greater than a certain value, simply use \(1\) minus the CDF. Finally, to compute the chance of being within a certain range, you can subtract the CDF of the smaller value, from the CDF of the larger value (see the examples below).









CautionExamples






RPython


If there are on average 5 falling stars in the sky every night, the chance of observing no more than 3 on a given night is equal to:

ppois(3, lambda = 5)

[1] 0.2650259


And the chance of observing at least 3 is equal to:

1 - ppois(2, lambda = 5)

[1] 0.875348


(This works because you start with 1 (100%) and exclude all options resulting in less than 3.)
To compute the probability of a certain range, just subtract the smaller value from the greater:

# Probability of 2 to 4 falling stars:
ppois(4, lambda = 5) - ppois(1, lambda = 5)

[1] 0.4000656


(This works because you start with all possibilities up till 4 and then exclude all options resulting in less than 2.)
The probability of a value of \(k \leq 3\) in Figure 3 is given by:

ppois(3, lambda = 3)

[1] 0.6472319




If there are on average 5 falling stars in the sky every night, the chance of observing no more than 3 on a given night is equal to:

from scipy.stats import poisson
y = poisson.cdf(3, 5)
print(y)

0.2650259152973615


And the chance of observing at least 3 is equal to:

y = 1 - poisson.cdf(2, 5)
print(y)

0.8753479805169189


(This works because you start with 1 (100%) and exclude all options resulting in less than 3.)
To compute the probability of a certain range, just subtract the smaller value from the greater:

# Probability of 2 to 4 falling stars:
y = poisson.cdf(4, 5) - poisson.cdf(1, 5)
print(y)

0.40006560307069977


(This works because you start with all possibilities up till 4 and then exclude all options resulting in less than 2.)
The probability of a value of \(k \leq 3\) in Figure 3 is given by:

y = poisson.cdf(3, 3)
print(y)

0.6472318887822313












Up till what point does the probability equal at least \(p\)?








Figure 4: Quantile function of a Poisson distribution with \(\lambda= 3\).






Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
  \tag{3}\label{qpois}
  \text{no simple closed form}
\end{align}\]


Code:


RPython



qpois(p, lambda)




from scipy.stats import poisson
poisson.ppf(p, mu)

Note: mu refers to the mean (\(\lambda\)).











TipExplanation





The quantile function is the inverse of the cumulative distribution function. It tells you up till what point the probability equals \(p\). To obtain the opposite—the point after which the probability equals a certain value, simply compute the quantile of \(1\) minus the probability (see the examples below).
There exists no simple expression for the quantile function of the Poisson distribution, but it can be computed anyway using a numeric search. If you are interested how this works, I explain it below.


If no simple closed form exists, how is it calculated?

The quantile function answers the opposite of the cumulative distribution function:

Cumulative distribution function: What is the probability \(p\) up till a certain count \(k\)?
Quantile function: What is the count \(k\) that has a probability of at least \(p\)?

This should give you a hint of how a numeric search might work: If you don’t have a quantile function, you can simply try plugging different \(k\)s in the cumulative distribution until you find the right answer.
Suppose that in Figure 4, you need to know the value for \(k\) that has a total probability of at least 80%:

# The real answer:
qpois(0.8, lambda = 3)

[1] 4

# A numeric search using the CDF:
k <- 0
p <- ppois(k, lambda = 3)
while(p < 0.8){
  k <- k + 1
  p <- ppois(k, lambda = 3)
}
print(k)

[1] 4


The search stops at \(k=4\), because that is the first instance of a probability of at least 80%.
There are more efficient ways to go about this, but this is the underlying principle of R’s qpois and Python’s poisson.ppf.










CautionExamples






RPython


If there are on average 5 falling stars each night, what is the largest number of falling stars for 95% of all nights?

qpois(0.95, lambda = 5)

[1] 9


Within what range is the number of falling stars on at least 95% of all nights?

qpois(c(0.025, 0.975), lambda = 5)

[1]  1 10


Apparently, at least 95% of nights would have 1–10 falling stars if the average were 5.


If there are on average 5 falling stars each night, what is the largest number of falling stars for 95% of all nights?

from scipy.stats import poisson
y = poisson.ppf(0.95, 5)
print(y)

9.0


Within what range is the number of falling stars on at least 95% of all nights?

y = poisson.ppf([0.025, 0.975], 5)
print(y)

[ 1. 10.]


Apparently, at least 95% of nights would have 1–10 falling stars if the average were 5.

title: Poisson Distribution
text:
Quiz

Question 1Answer


Perhaps the most commonly used laboratory animal is the mouse strain C57BL/6. A study from 2015 estimated its litter size1 to be approximately 7.5.[1]
1 The number of offspring born at one time.Assuming litter size can be reasonably approximated with a Poisson distribution, what would be the chance of a litter size of 3 or more?





C57BL/6 mouse. Source: jax.org/strain/003548










NoteHint





Use the code under Example in the probability mass function tab to plot the distribution. This is the best way to get a feel for it.









Now you can already see what would be a plausible answer: Almost all litter sizes are 3 or larger, so this should be well over 95%.
The question can be answered with the cumulative distribution function, see the explanation for details.









CautionTry it in browser






Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.





Use the complement of the cumulative distribution function:

RPython



1 - ppois(2, 7.5)

[1] 0.9797433





from scipy.stats import poisson
y = 1 - poisson.cdf(2, 7.5)
print(y)

0.9797432849433356





The cumulative distribution function gives you the left tail of the distribution. Hence, 1 minus the function gives you the right tail. This is called the complement.
If a Poisson distribution is a reasonable approximation, only about 2% of litters should be expected to have less than 3 mice.




Question 2Answer


Continuing on question 1, within what values would you expect 80% of all litter sizes to be?






NoteHint





This can be answered with the quantile function.









CautionTry it in browser






Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.





The central 80% lies between the 10th and 90th percentile:

RPython



qpois(c(0.1, 0.9), lambda = 7.5)

[1]  4 11





from scipy.stats import poisson
y = poisson.ppf([0.1, 0.9], 7.5)
print(y)

[ 4. 11.]





If a Poisson distribution is a reasonable approximation, the answer is 4–11 mice.

title: Binomial Distribution
text:
Properties
A discrete, probability distribution that can be left or right skewed.
The binomial distribution is the number of successes out of the number of trials. It is used to model ratios, fractions and binary data. If trials are independent and have a fixed probability of success \(p\), then the binomial distribution is not an approximation, but the probability distribution of ratios.
In reality, the probability of success may depend on unknown, unmeasured, or otherwise unaccounted for external factors: If we consider the effect of smoking on the probability of developing lung cancer, then such external factors might include familial history, exposure to other carcinogens, etc. For this reason, analyses based on a binomial distribution should include some assessment of whether the chosen distribution is realistic.

title: Binomial Distribution
text:
Probability mass functionCumulative distribution functionQuantile function



What is the probability of a given number of successes \(k\)?








Figure 1: Probability mass function of a binomial distribution with \(n = 10\) trials and \(p = 0.75\).






Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
  \tag{1}\label{dbinom}
  \binom{n}{k} p^k (1 - p)^{n - k}
\end{align}\]


Code:


RPython



dbinom(k, n, p)




from scipy.stats import binom
binom.pmf(k, n, p)












NoteSymbols






\(n\): The number of trials
\(k\): The number of successes
\(p\): The probability of success
\(x \choose y\): The binomial coefficient










TipExplanation





The binomial distribution is a discrete probability distribution. There are only \(n + 1\) possible values for the outcome (\(0, 1, 2, \dots, n\)). Hence, you can directly read probabilities off the \(y\)-axis in Figure 1.
The correct term for a probability function of a discrete distribution is a probability mass function, though it is common in literature to see people call both discrete and continuous versions a probability density function.
Note that while it looks like the probability is zero at \(k = 2\) or less in Figure 1, it is never exactly zero within the range of possible values. The probability is just too small to be visible in the figure.
The number of successes cannot be negative, nor larger than the number of trials. If \(p\) is close to zero or one, the remaining probability gets pressed up into the side. If you increase \(n\), or move \(p\) closer to a half, you move further away from zero, so this skew becomes less apparent:








Figure 2: Increasing \(n\), or moving \(p\) closer to \(0.5\) results in a more symmetric distribution.














CautionExample






RPython


The probability of \(k = 4\) in Figure 1 is:

dbinom(4, 10, 0.75)

[1] 0.016222


Using the following code, you can plot the probability mass function of binomial distribution with \(n = 10\) and \(p = 0.8\):

What is the probability up till a given point \(k\)?

Mathematical formula:

\(k\): The number of successes
\(p\): The probability of success

\(\sum\): Summation (compute for \(0, 1, \dots, k\) and add all results)










TipExplanation





The cumulative distribution function (CDF) is the sum of the probability mass function up till a given point \(k\). It can be used to calculate the probability of the number of successes being no greater than a certain value. To obtain the opposite—the chance of an observation greater than a certain value, simply use \(1\) minus the CDF. Finally, to compute the chance of being within a certain range, you can subtract the CDF of the smaller value, from the CDF of the larger value (see the examples below).









CautionExamples

\end{align}\]

RPython

print(y)












TipExplanation





The quantile function is the inverse of the cumulative distribution function. It tells you up till what point the probability equals \(p\). To obtain the opposite—the point after which the probability equals a certain value, simply compute the quantile of \(1\) minus the probability (see the examples below).
There exists no simple expression for the quantile function of the binomial distribution, but it can be computed anyway using a numeric search. If you are interested how this works, I explain it below.


If no simple closed form exists, how is it calculated?

The quantile function answers the opposite of the cumulative distribution function:

Cumulative distribution function: What is the probability \(p\) up till a certain number of successes \(k\)?
Quantile function: What is the number of successes \(k\) that has a probability of at least \(p\)?

This should give you a hint of how a numeric search might work: If you don’t have a quantile function, you can simply try plugging different \(k\)s in the cumulative distribution until you find the right answer.
Suppose that in Figure 4, you need to know the value for \(k\) that has a total probability of at least 80%:

# The real answer:

[1] 9

# A numeric search using the CDF:
k <- 0
p <- pbinom(k, 10, 0.75)
while(p < 0.8){
  k <- k + 1
  p <- pbinom(k, 10, 0.75)
}
print(k)

[1] 9


The search stops at \(k=9\), because that is the first instance of a probability of at least 80%.
There are more efficient ways to go about this, but this is the underlying principle of R’s qbinom and Python’s binom.ppf.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Procedure
Suppose we want to know the effect of a new compound on blood pressure. In a trial with 30 patients, blood pressure drops in some patients and rises in others. The average drop is 4.8 mmHg:
Is that enough evidence that the compound affects blood pressure? Blood pressure varies from patient to patient, and from day to day. Even if the medicine did nothing, the average change in 30 patients would not be exactly zero.
The question is therefore not whether the average differs from zero, but whether it differs more than we would expect if it did nothing. This is the fundamental idea behind a hypothesis test:
That frequency is a \(p\)-value. If it is small, our result would be surprising if there were no effect.
Hypothesis testing consists of these steps:
In the next sections, we explore how steps 4–6 work. For the \(t\)-value used in this example, step 4 first requires an estimate of the uncertainty: the standard error.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Choose a null hypothesis (\(H_0\)).
Choose a level of significance (\(\alpha\)).
Collect the data.
Calculate a test statistic.
Calculate the \(p\)-value.
Reject \(H_0\) if \(p \leq \alpha\). Otherwise, do not reject \(H_0\).







CautionExample: Blood pressure trial






\(H_0\!: \mu = 0\). The compound does not change blood pressure on average.
\(\alpha = 0.05\). We accept a 5% chance of a false positive. Typically, \(\alpha = 0.05\) is used unless specified otherwise. This choice is baked into science, but it is also arbitrary: There is nothing special about a 5% chance.
In \(n = 30\) patients, we found a mean of \(\bar{y} = -4.8\) mmHg and standard deviation of \(s = 9.7\) mmHg.
We can use the \(t\)-value, which is here the mean divided by its standard error: \(t = \frac{\bar{y}}{\mathrm{SE}_{\bar{y}}} = -2.7\).
If \(H_0\) were true, a \(t\)-value at least this far from zero occurs with probability \(p = 0.011\).
Since \(p \leq 0.05\), we reject \(H_0\): The average decrease of 4.8 mmHg is significantly non-zero.






Standard error
What is the uncertainty of our estimate?
The average change, \(\bar{y} = -4.8\) mmHg, is an estimate of the true mean change \(\mu\). With \(n=30\) new patients, we would have found a different mean. The extent to which estimates differ from each other in different samples is called the standard error.2
2 More precisely, the standard error of an estimate is the standard deviation of the estimates you would obtain by repeatedly sampling \(n\) observations from the same population.The most straightforward way to obtain a standard error would be to repeat the clinical trial many times and see how much the decrease in blood pressure varies across samples. Thankfully for our patients, that is not necessary if we have an analytic expression for the standard error. For the sample mean \(\bar{y}\), we have such an expression:
\[\begin{align}
  \label{trueSEM}
  \tag{1}\mathrm{SE}_{\bar{y}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\end{align}\]
In practice, we do not know \(\sigma\), so we can estimate the standard error, by plugging in an estimate \(s\):
\[\begin{align}
  \label{SEM}
  \tag{2}\hat{\mathrm{SE}}_{\bar{y}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\end{align}\]
The standard error is small if patients differ little from each other (small \(s\)), or if there are many patients (large \(n\)). Because of the square root, there are diminishing returns: To halve the standard error, you need four times as many patients.
For our clinical trial, the standard error is \(\frac{9.7}{\sqrt{30}} = 1.77\) mmHg.


Test statistic
How far is our estimate from \(H_0\)?
Is a decrease of 4.8 mmHg far from zero? This can be expressed with a test statistic. For a sample mean, we can use the \(t\)-value:
\[\begin{align}
  \label{t}
  \tag{3}t = \frac{\bar{y} - \mu_0}{\mathrm{SE}},
\end{align}\]
where \(\mu_0\) is the value under the null hypothesis.3 From the formula, you can see that the \(t\)-value is large if there is a large drop in blood pressure, and if the uncertainty of the estimate is small. The \(t\)-value is essentially \(\frac{\text{difference from zero}}{\text{uncertainty}}\). The further \(t\) is from zero, the less compatible the data are with \(H_0\).
3 We can in principle compare our estimate to any number. Often, however, asking “Is there an effect?” is the same as asking “Does it differ from zero?”For our clinical trial, the \(t\)-value is \(\frac{-4.8 - 0}{1.77} = -2.71\).


\(p\)-value
How far from \(H_0\) is far enough?
If \(H_0\) is true, and we make certain assumptions,4 \(t\)-values follow a known distribution: a \(t\)-distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom.5 Most \(t\)-values are then close to zero, and values far from zero are rare. The \(p\)-value is the probability of a \(t\)-value at least as far from zero as ours, if \(H_0\) is true.
4 In this case, independent observations and normally distributed errors. The errors are here simply the differences from the mean.5 The \(t\)-distribution resembles the  normal distribution, but has heavier tails. These account for the extra uncertainty of estimating \(\sigma\) by \(s\). With more observations, \(s\) becomes more precise, and the \(t\)-distribution approaches the normal distribution.There is no single formula to compute a \(p\)-value: it depends on the test statistic and its distribution under \(H_0\). For the \(t\)-value, it is the area under the curve beyond the observed value, in both directions:








Figure 2: Distribution of the \(t\)-value if \(H_0\) is true (\(t\)-distribution with 29 degrees of freedom). The dotted line marks the observed \(t\)-value. The blue area is the probability of a \(t\)-value at least this far from zero (the \(p\)-value).





For our clinical trial, \(p = 0.011\) (the shaded area in Figure 2). At \(\alpha = 0.05\), we would reject \(H_0\) and conclude there is a significant decrease. Had \(p\) been larger than \(\alpha\), we would not have rejected \(H_0\), and concluded the decrease was not significant.






NoteWhy both directions?





In the example provided here, the question was what the effect of the compound is. A fair test should therefore consider both the potential to raise, or lower blood pressure. A one-sided test, which checks only one direction, can be justified if an effect in the other direction would lead to the same decision as no effect. For example, if we measure a contaminant in drinking water to see whether it exceeds the legal limit, then water at the limit and water far below it call for the same decision: no action. Be careful though, like other analysis decisions, the direction must be chosen before looking at the data. Choosing it afterward would double the false positive rate.





Confidence interval
Which values are plausible?
A \(p\)-value only tells us whether one particular value (\(\mu_0 = 0\)) can be rejected. A confidence interval shows a range of plausible values for the true mean \(\mu\). It is good practice to report not only the \(p\)-value, but also the effect size and a 95% confidence interval.






NoteWhy 95% confidence intervals?





If you set a significance level of \(\alpha\), that corresponds to constructing a \((1 - \alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval. Since \(\alpha = 0.05\) is commonly used, so are 95% confidence intervals.
Note that this 95% describes the method, not a single interval: If the trial were repeated many times, 95% of the intervals would contain the true mean \(\mu\). “Range of plausible values” is a rough interpretation. The precise definition is surprisingly unintuitive, and beyond the scope of this chapter. For an explanation, please refer to the  video on confidence intervals.



For our clinical trial, the 95% confidence interval runs from -8.4 to -1.2 mmHg. Zero lies outside it, which here corresponds to \(p \leq 0.05\). Unlike the \(p\)-value, however, the interval also shows how large the effect could plausibly be.
Whether an effect matters in practice is a subject-matter judgment, not a statistical one (e.g., a drop of less than 5 mmHg may not be worth taking a medicine). Once that is decided, the interval can distinguish situations that a \(p\)-value cannot:








Figure 3: Four hypothetical studies. Points are estimates, lines are 95% confidence intervals. The gray area marks effects smaller than \(\delta\), the smallest effect that matters in practice.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Error rates
A test can make two types of errors: A false positive (rejecting \(H_0\) even though it is true) and a false negative (not rejecting \(H_0\) even though it is false). These error rates are related as follows:









\(H_0\) is false
\(H_0\) is true




\(p \leq \alpha\)
True positive (\(1 - \beta\))
False positive (\(\alpha\))


\(p > \alpha\)
False negative (\(\beta\))
True negative (\(1 - \alpha\))



The probability of a true positive, \(1 - \beta\), is called the power of a test: its ability to detect a real difference from \(H_0\). Unlike \(\alpha\), power is not directly chosen. It depends on the size of the true effect, \(\alpha\), \(n\) and the variance. Power calculations (for very simple tests) and simulation (for anything else) can be used to determine an appropriate sample size to attain a certain power.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Limitations of hypothesis testing
Hypothesis testing is ubiquitous in science, which is why it is important that you understand statistical significance, power, and false positives/negatives. It is also a highly criticized practice, because it is very susceptible to misuse.

A test is never conclusive. Even if \(H_0\) is true, it rejects with probability \(\alpha\), and even if \(H_0\) is false, it may fail to reject. \(H_0\) can be shown to be implausible, but never strictly disproven.
A test relies on assumptions (e.g., independent observations). If these do not hold, the \(p\)-value loses its meaning. (These will be covered in the following chapters.)
A test relies on a fixed plan. The hypotheses, \(\alpha\) and the analysis must be chosen before looking at the data. Otherwise, \(p\)-values and \(\alpha\) lose their meaning.

In addition, a lot of misuse stems from misunderstanding \(p\)-values and confidence intervals. Hence, the list below contains some of the most common misconceptions.






ImportantCommon misconceptions about \(p\)-values





Misinterpretations of \(p\)-values are widespread [1]–[5]. Below are some of the most frequent, based on published research and surveys of researchers [6]–[9].

“If \(p > 0.05\), there is no effect.”

Absence of evidence is not proof of absence. The effect may be too small to detect with this sample size. If the confidence interval includes effects that would matter in practice, the study is inconclusive. Only if the interval excludes all effects that would matter can we conclude that any effect is negligible, which is the idea behind equivalence testing.

“The \(p\)-value is the probability that \(H_0\) is true.”

The \(p\)-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, computed assuming that \(H_0\) and all other model assumptions are true. It is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true given the data. Compare a diagnostic test: the probability of a positive result in a healthy patient is not the probability that a patient with a positive result is healthy.

“If \(p < 0.05\), there is at most a 5% chance of a false positive.”

\(\alpha = 0.05\) is the chance of a significant result if \(H_0\) is true. The chance that a significant result is a false positive also depends on how often the tested effects are different from \(H_0\), and on power [3].

“The \(p\)-value is the probability that the result is due to chance alone.”

The \(p\)-value is computed by assuming that chance alone, under \(H_0\) and the model, produced the data. It cannot also be the probability of that assumption. This is a variant of the claim that the \(p\)-value is the probability that \(H_0\) is true.

“\(1 - p\) is the probability that a replication will be significant.”

The chance that a replication is significant is its power, which depends on the unknown true effect. Suppose the true effect equals the observed one and the original study had \(p = 0.05\). Then a replication of the same size is significant only about half the time [10].

“One study is significant and another is not, so their results contradict each other.”

The difference between significant and not significant is not itself necessarily significant [8], [11]. To compare two studies, estimate the difference between their effects and its confidence interval. Discordant results are expected even when both studies estimate the same effect. If two independent studies each have power \(1 - \beta\), the chance that exactly one is significant is \(2\beta(1-\beta)\). At 50% power, they disagree half the time.

“A smaller \(p\)-value means a larger or more important effect.”

The \(p\)-value depends on the size of the effect, its variability, and the sample size. With enough data, any nonzero effect, however negligible, is significant. The estimate and its confidence interval show the size of the effect. Whether that size matters is a subject-matter judgment.

“Out of many tests, the significant ones are the important ones.”

Significance does not indicate importance, as above. Moreover, even if \(H_0\) is true, each test has a chance of \(\alpha\) of being significant. With \(k\) independent tests of true null hypotheses, the chance of at least one false positive is \(1 - (1 - \alpha)^k\). For example, among 10 comparisons, that chance is already over 40%. Without multiple testing correction, false positives are therefore likely. And estimates selected because they are significant are biased upward, especially when power is low [12].











ImportantCommon misconceptions about confidence intervals






“95% of the observations lie in the confidence interval.”

A confidence interval shows the uncertainty in an estimate, like the sample mean \(\bar{y}\), not the spread of the observations. As the sample size grows, the interval narrows, but the observations remain as spread out as before.

“There is a 95% probability that the true value lies in this interval.”

The 95% describes the method, not a single interval: If the study were repeated many times, 95% of the intervals would contain the true value. A single interval either contains it or not, and we cannot tell which.

“Values inside the interval are plausible, values outside it are ruled out.”

The boundaries are no sharper than the significance level they come from. Values just outside the interval are hardly less compatible with the data than values just inside it.

“If two confidence intervals overlap, the difference between them is not significant.”

Two 95% confidence intervals can overlap while the difference between the estimates is significant. To compare two estimates, look at the confidence interval of their difference.

“A narrow interval means the estimate is accurate.”

The interval only reflects sampling variation, and only if the model assumptions hold. It says nothing about bias, for example from a flawed study design.


For the precise meaning of a confidence interval, please refer to the  video on confidence intervals.

title: Simple Linear Regression
text:
Linear regression with a single explanatory variable.

This part introduces the basics of regression analysis, which we will then use for estimation, comparisons, and prediction.
This part is split into two chapters:

Ordinary Linear Models (regression of continuous outcomes with a central tendency)
Generalized Linear Models (regression of counts, ratios, binary outcomes, and more)

To get started, watch the videos on ordinary linear models.
These are the most information-dense chapters of the website. Take your time to familiarize yourself with the contents. Both chapters end with interactive apps to test your knowledge, and the ultimate goal: A full analysis for you to do in RStudio.






TipWhat level of detail do I need for the exam?





If you are using this book in the context of one of my courses, please note the following:

On the exam, you interpret these models from their regression table. Focus on what the intercept and slope mean, and what you can conclude from their p-values and confidence intervals.
You judge the assumptions from diagnostic plots. Know what each plot is used for and what clear violations look like.
For generalized linear models, know which distribution suits which type of outcome (continuous, counts, ratios, binary), what causes overdispersion, and how to interpret the output of a GLM.
You do not need to memorize technical definitions in the summaries, such as the natural parameter and the canonical link function.

1.2 Summary








Figure 1.1: Example of a simple linear model. (Height and weight of 30 individuals.)






Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
  y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x + \epsilon \\ \tag{1}\label{slm}\\
  \epsilon &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \, \sigma^2)
\end{align}\]


Code:


RPython



model <- lm(y ~ x, data)




import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
model = smf.ols("y ~ x", data).fit()












NoteSymbols & definitions






\(y\) — response variable

The outcome.


\(\hat{y}\) is the predicted outcome by the model, also called the ‘fitted value.’

\(x\) — explanatory variable

The variable the outcome is regressed on.

\(\beta_0\) — intercept

Mean of the outcome (\(y\)), when the explanatory variable (\(x\)) is zero.


\(\beta_0\) is the theoretical value.


\(\hat{\beta}_0\) is its estimate.

\(\beta_1\) — slope

Change in the mean of the outcome (\(y\)), when the explanatory variable (\(x\)) increases by one.


\(\beta_1\) is the theoretical value.


\(\hat{\beta}_1\) is its estimate.

\(\epsilon\) — error

Difference between the true population values of the outcome and those predicted by the true model.


\(\epsilon\) is the true error.


\(\hat{\epsilon}\) is sometimes used to denote the residual, an ‘estimate’ of the error.

\(\mathcal{N}\) — normal distribution

See  Normal Distribution.


\(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \, \sigma^2)\) means: The error follows a normal distribution with mean \(\mu = 0\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) (some unknown variance).











TipExplanation





Simple linear regression models the relationship between two continuous variables, using an intercept and a slope:








Figure 1.2: The intercept is the value of \(y\), when \(x=0\). The slope is the average change in \(y\), when \(x\) increases by \(1\).





A model is only an approximation and there will always be individual differences from the ‘average’ trend that has been estimated. These differences are called the residuals:








Figure 1.3: Residual of a simple linear model.






The intercept and slope are estimated by minimizing the sum of squared residuals, a technique called ordinary least squares. In contrast to the many adaptations that exist, like weighted least squares, partial least squares, etc.








Figure 1.4: Squared residuals give proportionally more weight to farther observations.






A simple linear model makes several key assumptions which are required for valid inference:

The observations are independent.
The relationship between the outcome and the explanatory variable is linear.
The error follows a normal distribution.
The error has a constant variance along the regression line.

And while not really an assumption, also important:

There are no influential outliers with unreasonably large influence on the estimates.

Independent measurements must be apparent from the study design. The rest can be checked through visual diagnostics. A quick visual summary of what each plot is used for:

These are the data of Figure 1.1. The estimated intercept is given by (Intercept) (132.15): The mean height at a weight of \(0\) kg. This lies far outside the range of the data, so it has no practical meaning; it only positions the line. The estimated slope is given by weight (0.5): For every additional kg of weight, height is on average 0.5 cm greater. Apparently, this slope differs significantly from zero (\(p = 1.78 \times 10^{-4}\)). Weight explains 40% of the total variance in height (Multiple R-squared).
The interactive app at the end of the chapter lets you hover over elements of the regression table and see what they mean.
For a complete analysis, refer to the tutorial at the bottom of the page.









ImportantHandling outliers





First, realize that outliers can also appear due to other underlying issues, as explained in the  fourth video. If you are sure the issue is outlyingness, I recommend these steps in order:

Look up the observation in the dataset.

Is the value plausible? (e.g., a negative height is not possible)
Does it stand out in other ways? (e.g., also unusual in terms of location, time, etc.)
Check any field notes, logs, or metadata. (e.g., a sample accidentally left out overnight)

If the value is valid, but outlying:

Consider modifying the model. (e.g., add a non-linear term or spline)
If changing the model is not appropriate—perhaps because there is strong theoretical foundation to assume a linear relationship—consider using robust standard errors. (e.g., the sandwich package in R)

Only remove the observation if:

It is clearly invalid. (e.g., misplaced decimal separator)
There is strong contextual evidence that it is not representative of the rest of the data.(e.g., a single patient of advanced age)


Inexperienced analysts are often quick to filter and discard observations, impute missing values, etc., but these are dangerous actions that can severely bias statistical inference. Handling outliers is not beginner stuff. Approach decisions with caution, or consult with an expert.

1.3 Quiz

Question 1Answer


Which of the following is implicitly assumed in simple linear regression? (choose one)
A. The data are normally distributed
B. The outcome is normally distributed
C. The errors are normally distributed
D. The response variable is normally distributed






NoteHint





See equation \(\eqref{slm}\).





Which of the following is implicitly assumed in simple linear regression? (choose one)
A. The data are normally distributed
B. The outcome is normally distributed
C. The errors are normally distributed
D. The response variable is normally distributed






TipLearn why





The normality assumption is about the error, the vertical distances along the regression line. Our ‘estimate’ of the error is called the residual.
Simple linear regression makes no assumptions about your entire data set, nor your outcome variable. Response variable is just a synonym for outcome.

Another correct way to phrase the assumption is that the outcome is conditionally normally distributed. The condition here is the value of the explanatory variable. Namely, we can rewrite equation \(\eqref{slm}\) as follows:
\[\begin{align}
  y \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x, \, \sigma^2)
\end{align}\]
This says: “The outcome follows a normal distribution with a mean that depends on the value of \(x\).”
Don’t worry if you do not fully understand this yet, as it will be covered at length in the next chapter.







Question 2Answer


In the context of simple linear regression, a confidence interval shows:
A. Where to expect current observations
B. Where to expect future observations
C. A plausible range of values for the intercept and slope
D. A 95% confidence interval has a 95% chance to contain the true intercept/slope






NoteHint





This is mentioned in the  first video, and more thoroughly explained in a separate video:

 Open video in a new tab





In the context of simple linear regression, a confidence interval shows:
A. Where to expect current observations
B. Where to expect future observations
C. A plausible range of values for the intercept and slope
D. A 95% confidence interval has a 95% chance to contain the true intercept/slope






TipLearn why





A. You don’t need an interval for this, just look at the observations.
B. This is the interpretation of a prediction interval.
C. This is a loose interpretation of a confidence interval, I recommend using. Purists may object to this definition, but as shown at the end of the video on confidence intervals, this interpretation is often very reasonable for the types of models you will learn about in this course.
D. This is the interpretation of a Bayesian credible interval.

2.2 Summary

NormalPoissonBinomial











Figure 2.1: Example of a simple linear model. (Height and weight of 50 individuals.)






Mathematical formula:


As ordinary LMAs GLM


\[\begin{align}
  \label{lm}
  y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x + \epsilon \\ \tag{1a}\\
  \epsilon &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \, \sigma^2)
\end{align}\]


\[\begin{align}
  \label{glmnorm}
  y|x &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \, \sigma^2)  \\ \\
  \mu &= \eta\tag{1b}\\ \\
  \eta &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x
\end{align}\]





Code:


RPython



model <- lm(y ~ x, data)




import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
model = smf.ols("y ~ x", data).fit()












NoteSymbols & definitions






\(y\) — response variable

The outcome.

\(x\) — explanatory variable

The variable the outcome is regressed on.

\(y|x\) — conditional response variable

The outcome at a given value of \(x\). (Read: \(y\) given \(x\).)

\(\mathcal{N}\) — normal distribution

See  Normal Distribution. \(y|x \sim \mathcal{N}\! \left(\mu, \, \sigma^2\right)\) means: The outcome follows a conditional normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). It is called conditional, because \(\mu\) is not a fixed number, but depends on \(x\).

\(\theta\) — natural parameter

The parameter in which the formula of the distribution is written in a GLM. Only needed here, to explain what makes the canonical link canonical.


More

A GLM involves three quantities: the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), the mean (\(\mu\)), and the natural parameter (\(\theta\)). The link function connects \(\eta\) to \(\mu\), and the distribution itself connects \(\theta\) to \(\mu\). With the canonical link, these two connections cancel out, so the linear predictor is that parameter: \(\eta = \theta\). With any other link, there is an extra conversion step in between. See also here.


link function

A function that stretches the possible range of the mean of the distribution from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\). This ensures the model can only predict valid values.

canonical link function

The one link function for which the linear predictor is the natural parameter (\(\eta=\theta\)). For the normal distribution, the natural parameter is the mean itself, so the canonical link is the identity function, which amounts to doing nothing. No transformation is needed anyway, because the mean of a normal distribution can already take on any value.

\(\eta\) — linear predictor

The linear combination of the explanatory variables and their coefficients.

\(\beta_0\) — intercept

Mean of the outcome (\(y\)), when the explanatory variable (\(x\)) is zero. \(\hat{\beta}_0\) (beta-hat) is its estimate.

\(\beta_1\) — slope

Change in the mean of the outcome (\(y\)), when the explanatory variable (\(x\)) increases by one. \(\hat{\beta}_1\) (beta-hat) is its estimate.











TipExplanation





Ordinary linear models are a special case of generalized linear models (GLMs). Whereas the former only support normally distributed errors, GLMs can handle any probability distribution in the exponential dispersion family.
To understand GLMs, try to let go of the idea that a linear model is \(\text{linear function} + \text{error}\), and instead take on a different perspective: A GLM is a probability distribution with a mean that depends on the explanatory variable (\(x\)). The technical term for this is conditional normality: If we know the value of the \(x\), then at that point, the outcome follows a normal distribution. Move to a different value of \(x\) and the mean of the distribution changes. This concept is visualized in the  first video on GLM.
Once we take on the perspective of a conditional probability distribution for the outcome, we can easily swap that distribution with another one, like Poisson or binomial. The only missing piece to do this is called the link function. Its purpose is to ensure the linear function will always output valid values (e.g., counts cannot be negative). If the link function is the one for which the linear predictor equals the natural parameter of the chosen probability distribution, it is called the canonical link function.
In the case of a normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}\! \left(\mu, \, \sigma^2\right)\), the mean \(\mu\) can already take on any value from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\), so no such translation is needed and we use what is called the identity function (it simply outputs the same value as the input). This is the middle line of the formula As GLM: \(\mu = \eta\). Since the natural parameter of the normal distribution is the mean itself, the identity link function is canonical.


When would you use a normal GLM with non-canonical link?

It is possible to use different link functions for a normal GLM (e.g., the logarithm). This is not the same as simply transforming the outcome. Below is an overview contrasting both methods.

Difference between log-transforming the outcome and using a log-link function.








LM with \(\log(y)\) as outcome
Normal GLM with log-link




Rationale
You expect the outcome (including the errors) to grow exponentially with the explanatory variable. Errors grow larger as \(y\) increases.
You expect the trend (excluding errors) to be exponential. Error variance is constant along this trend.


Example
Someone who spends $100 on average will have smaller absolute spread in spending than someone who spends $1,000 on average.
A deterministic process like laser intensity as a function of distance still has measurement error. This can cause a constant spread along an exponential relationship.


Disadvantage
Transforming back to the original scale is not straightforward, due to retransformation bias and requires e.g., a smearing estimate [1].
Less common in practice. In most real-world processes, if something grows exponentially, its spread tends to grow exponentially too.













CautionExample





An ordinary linear model (LM) is a special case of a generalized linear model (GLM). Compare the output of both forms, fitted to the data of Figure 2.1:

The \(p\)-values and confidence intervals would then differ slightly from those of ols, and from those of R.






Both methods produce identical estimates and standard errors, demonstrating that a normal GLM is not fundamentally different from an ordinary linear model.

RPython


Differences between lm and glm include:

lm shows a simple summary of the residuals, glm does not. This is because GLMs are not limited to normally distributed errors, so it does not necessarily help to inspect the residuals. (For distributions other than normal, there is no possible decomposition into \(\text{linear function} + \text{error}\).)
lm always shows a \(t\)-value. glm shows a \(t\)-value for some distributions and a \(z\)-value for others (particularly Poisson and binomial). The reason for this is a bit technical, but it boils down to whether the spread of the outcome had to be estimated from the data. For the normal distribution it does (\(\sigma^2\)), so glm shows \(t\)-values here too. For Poisson and binomial GLMs, the spread follows from the mean, nothing extra is estimated, and glm shows \(z\)-values. A longer explanation is included at the end.
lm shows \(R^2\) and \(R^2_{\mathrm{adjusted}}\), a GLM does not. This is because GLMs do not explain variance (\(\sigma^2\)), but a more broad definition of spread, called deviance.
glm does not show the residual standard deviation for the same reason.
lm includes an omnibus \(F\)-test. This test is not suitable for GLMs, so it is not included in the output of glm.
glm shows the null and residual deviance. Deviance is a measure of spread that applies more generally than the variance (\(\sigma^2\)).

This gives you a similar piece of information as \(R^2\) does in lm: There was originally a deviance of 3320.4, of which 3191.9 is left.
In the special case of a normal GLM, the deviance explained coincides with the variance explained: \(1 - \frac{3191.9}{3320.4} = 3.9\%\), again showing that an ordinary linear model is the same as a normal GLM with identity link.

glm shows the Akaike information criterion (AIC) value by default, lm does not. This difference is superficial, as AIC is well-defined for both models (try AIC(LM)). Note that this number is useless in isolation—it is only useful when comparing models.
At the bottom, glm shows the number of iterations it took for the fitting procedure to converge, by means of Fisher scoring. This is a fast method for obtaining the estimates of a GLM, which is not used in lm.



Differences between ols and glm include:

ols shows tests and statistics of the residuals (Omnibus, Jarque-Bera, Durbin-Watson, Skew, Kurtosis), glm does not. This is because GLMs are not limited to normally distributed errors, so it does not necessarily help to inspect the residuals. Either way, the assumptions are better checked visually, as shown in the previous chapter.
ols shows \(R^2\) and \(R^2_{\mathrm{adjusted}}\), glm does not. Instead, glm shows a pseudo \(R^2\) (Pseudo R-squ. (CS)), a measure based on the likelihood that mimics \(R^2\). For a normal GLM, it is practically the same as \(R^2\).
ols includes an omnibus \(F\)-test. This test is not suitable for GLMs, so it is not included in the output of glm.
glm shows Scale, which for a normal GLM is the estimated variance (\(\hat{\sigma}^2 = 66.5\)). Its square root is the residual standard deviation (\(\hat{\sigma} = 8.15\)), which neither output shows.
glm shows the residual deviance (Deviance), but not the null deviance. The latter is stored in GLM.null_deviance. As in R, \(1 - \frac{3191.9}{3320.4} = 3.9\%\) of the deviance is explained, the same as \(R^2\).
ols shows the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), glm does not. Its AIC is stored in GLM.aic. Note that R counts \(\sigma^2\) as one more parameter, so the AIC of R is always \(2\) higher than that of statsmodels. Only compare AIC values computed in the same way.
glm shows the number of iterations it took for the fitting procedure to converge (No. Iterations), by means of iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS), the same procedure that R calls Fisher scoring. This is a fast method for obtaining the estimates of a GLM, which is not used in ols.






Technical explanation: \(t\)-values vs \(z\)-values

The test statistic (\(t\) or \(z\)) of a regression table is an estimate divided by its standard error. This standard error depends on the spread of the outcome:

If the spread is presumed known, the statistic is compared to a normal distribution (a \(z\)-value). This is the case for Poisson (\(\text{mean}=\text{variance}=\lambda\)) and binomial (\(\text{variance}= np(1-p)\)).
If the spread is estimated, this adds uncertainty. The statistic is then compared to a \(t\)-distribution with the residual degrees of freedom, whose heavier tails account for that extra uncertainty. This is the case for normal, but also gamma, quasi-Poisson and quasi-binomial GLMs.

Try for example, fitting one of the Poisson GLM examples with family = "quasipoisson". The \(z\)-values become \(t\)-values, because the dispersion is now estimated separately.
The \(t\)-distribution is exact only for the normal distribution. For all other GLMs, both \(t\) and \(z\) are large-sample approximations. In practice, model assumptions rarely hold exactly. Hence, this technical difference is not so important, and there also exist better, more general methods of obtaining \(p\)-values and confidence intervals, like bootstrapping.

How to interpret the estimates themselves is shown in the Example of the previous chapter. For a complete analysis, refer to the tutorial of the previous chapter.















Figure 2.2: Example of Poisson regression. (Apples per year as a function of tree age.)






Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
  \label{glmpois}
  y|x &\sim \mathsf{Pois}(\lambda)  \\ \\
  \tag{2}\log(\lambda) &= \eta \\ \\
  \eta &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x
\end{align}\]


Code:


RPython



model <- glm(y ~ x, data, family = "poisson")




import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
model = smf.glm("y ~ x", data, family = sm.families.Poisson()).fit()












NoteSymbols & definitions






\(y\) — response variable

The outcome.

\(x\) — explanatory variable

The variable the outcome is regressed on.

\(y|x\) — conditional response variable

The outcome at a given value of \(x\). (Read: \(y\) given \(x\).)

\(\mathsf{Pois}\) — Poisson distribution

See  Poisson Distribution. \(y|x \sim \mathsf{Pois}(\lambda)\) means: The outcome follows a conditional Poisson distribution with rate \(\lambda\). It is called conditional, because \(\lambda\) is not a fixed number, but depends on \(x\).

\(\theta\) — natural parameter

The parameter in which the formula of the distribution is written in a GLM. Only needed here, to explain what makes the canonical link canonical.


More

A GLM involves three quantities: the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), the mean (\(\mu\)), and the natural parameter (\(\theta\)). The link function connects \(\eta\) to \(\mu\), and the distribution itself connects \(\theta\) to \(\mu\). With the canonical link, these two connections cancel out, so the linear predictor is that parameter: \(\eta = \theta\). With any other link, there is an extra conversion step in between. See also here.


link function

A function that stretches the possible range of the mean of the distribution from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\). This ensures the model can only predict valid values. For a Poisson GLM, that means non-negative counts.

canonical link function

The one link function for which the linear predictor is the natural parameter (\(\eta=\theta\)). For the Poisson distribution, this is the natural logarithm: \(\log(\lambda)\).

\(\eta\) — linear predictor

The linear combination of the explanatory variables and their coefficients.

\(\beta_0\) — intercept

Value of the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when the explanatory variable (\(x\)) is zero. \(\hat{\beta}_0\) (beta-hat) is its estimate. For a Poisson GLM with log-link, \(\exp(\beta_0)\) is the mean count at \(x=0\).

\(\beta_1\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when the explanatory variable (\(x\)) increases by one. \(\hat{\beta}_1\) (beta-hat) is its estimate. For a Poisson GLM with log-link, \(\exp(\beta_1)\) is the multiplicative change in mean count when \(x\) increases by \(1\) (see:  GLM Regression Table).











TipExplanation





A Poisson GLM is used to model count data. It is the model of choice when counts are truly independent and occur at a fixed rate—that is, when the rate depends only on the explanatory variable (\(x\)).
In a Poisson GLM, we estimate the rate of occurrence (\(\lambda\)). Since events cannot occur at a negative rate, a suitable link function must ensure \(\lambda \geq 0\). A common choice is the natural logarithm \(\log(\lambda) = \eta\), because it implies \(\lambda = e^{\eta}\) (always positive). This is also the canonical link function of a Poisson GLM. An example of a non-canonical link function is the square root \(\sqrt{\lambda} = \eta\).
In practice, counts are often correlated, zero-inflated, or otherwise not truly independent and occurring at a fixed rate. For an explanation of this topic, as well as alternatives to Poisson regression, refer to the  fourth video on GLM.

The estimates are on the scale of the link function (the logarithm), so to interpret them, we transform them back with \(\exp\). The estimated intercept is given by (Intercept) (\(\hat{\beta}_0 = -0.89\)): A tree of age \(0\) would carry on average \(\exp(\hat{\beta}_0) = 0.41\) apples, but this lies outside the range of the data. The estimated slope is given by x (\(\hat{\beta}_1 = 1.25\)): Every additional year of age multiplies the mean number of apples by \(\exp(\hat{\beta}_1) = 3.48\). NoteSymbols & definitions






\(y\) — response variable

The outcome.

\(x\) — explanatory variable

The variable the outcome is regressed on.

\(y|x\) — conditional response variable

The outcome at a given value of \(x\). (Read: \(y\) given \(x\).)

\(\mathsf{Binom}\) — binomial distribution

See  Binomial Distribution. \(y|x \sim \mathsf{Binom}(n, \, p)\) means: The outcome follows a conditional binomial distribution with \(n\) trials and probability of success \(p\). It is called conditional, because \(p\) is not a fixed number, but depends on \(x\).

\(\mathsf{Bernoulli}\) — Bernoulli distribution

A binomial distribution with one trial simplifies to what is called the Bernoulli distribution.

\(\theta\) — natural parameter

The parameter in which the formula of the distribution is written in a GLM. Only needed here, to explain what makes the canonical link canonical.


More

A GLM involves three quantities: the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), the mean (\(\mu\)), and the natural parameter (\(\theta\)). The link function connects \(\eta\) to \(\mu\), and the distribution itself connects \(\theta\) to \(\mu\). With the canonical link, these two connections cancel out, so the linear predictor is that parameter: \(\eta = \theta\). With any other link, there is an extra conversion step in between. See also here.


link function

A function that stretches the possible range of the mean of the distribution from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\). This ensures the model can only predict valid values. For a binomial GLM, that means probabilities between \(0\) and \(1\).

canonical link function

The one link function for which the linear predictor is the natural parameter (\(\eta=\theta\)). For the binomial distribution, this is the logarithm of the odds, or logit: \(\log \left( \frac{p}{1-p} \right)\).

\(\eta\) — linear predictor

The linear combination of the explanatory variables and their coefficients.

\(\beta_0\) — intercept

Value of the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when the explanatory variable (\(x\)) is zero. \(\hat{\beta}_0\) (beta-hat) is its estimate. For a binomial GLM with logit-link, \(\exp(\beta_0)\) is the odds at \(x=0\).

\(\beta_1\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when the explanatory variable (\(x\)) increases by one. \(\hat{\beta}_1\) (beta-hat) is its estimate. For a binomial GLM with logit-link, \(\exp(\beta_1)\) is the multiplicative change in odds when \(x\) increases by \(1\) (see:  GLM Regression Table). No direct interpretation in terms of probability is possible.











TipExplanation





A binomial GLM is used to model ratios and binary outcomes. It is the model of choice when the trials are truly independent and the probability of success fixed—that is, when the probability of success depends only on the explanatory variable (\(x\)).
In a binomial GLM, we estimate the probability of success (\(p\)). Since probabilities must be within \(0\) and \(1\), a suitable link function must ensure \(0 \leq p \leq 1\). A common choice is the logit \[\log\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right) = \eta \quad \implies \quad p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\eta}}\] which is between \(0\) and \(1\) for any value of \(\eta\). This is also the canonical link function of a binomial GLM. Examples of non-canonical link functions include the probit \(\Phi^{-1}(p) = \eta\) and the complementary log-log \(\log(-\log(1 - p)) = \eta\).
Often, trials are correlated or otherwise not truly independent and occurring with a fixed probability of success. For an explanation of this topic, as well as alternatives to binomial regression, refer to the  fourth video on GLM.
Finally, if you have the choice—such as during the study design phase—always use the original number of successes and failures, not a percentage or proportion. Computing a percentage discards valuable information (i.e., the number of trials).

The estimates are on the scale of the link function (the logit), so to interpret them, we transform them back with \(\exp\), which gives odds. The estimated intercept is given by (Intercept) (\(\hat{\beta}_0 = -3.96\)): Without studying, the odds of a correct answer are \(\exp(\hat{\beta}_0) = 0.02\). The estimated slope is given by x (\(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0.37\)): Every additional hour of studying multiplies the odds of a correct answer by \(\exp(\hat{\beta}_1) = 1.45\). text:
2.3 Quiz

Question 1Answer


Which of the following is implicitly assumed in a generalized linear model? (choose one)
A. The data follow a distribution in the exponential dispersion family
B. The outcome follows a distribution in the exponential dispersion family
C. The residuals follow a distribution in the exponential dispersion family
D. The outcome conditionally follows a distribution in the exponential dispersion family






NoteHint





See the  first video on GLM.





Which of the following is implicitly assumed in a generalized linear model? (choose one)
A. The data follow a distribution in the exponential dispersion family
B. The outcome follows a distribution in the exponential dispersion family
C. The residuals follow a distribution in the exponential dispersion family
D. The outcome conditionally follows a distribution in the exponential dispersion family






TipLearn why





The distributional assumption is about the conditional outcome, which means: At any given value of the explanatory variable (\(x\)), the outcome is assumed to follow the specified distribution. But the unconditional outcome (disregarding the value of \(x\)) is not assumed to follow anything.
In mathematical terms,
\[\begin{aligned}

y &\not\sim \text{probability distribution} \\ \\

y|x &\sim \text{probability distribution}

\end{aligned}\]
GLMs make no assumptions about your entire data set, nor your outcome variable. The residuals are also irrelevant, as a GLM has no error term in its equation. The randomness instead comes from the specified probability distribution.







Question 2Answer


Which probability distributions are associated with these processes?

The number of bees visiting flowers in one minute.
The number of germinated seeds in a pot, out of 20 planted.
Cortisol concentration in blood plasma samples (ng/mL).
Presence or absence of sharks in different locations.







NoteHint





Choose from among: normal, Poisson, Bernoulli, binomial.





Which probability distributions are associated with these processes?

The number of bees visiting flowers in one minute. Poisson
The number of germinated seeds in a pot, out of 20 planted. binomial
Cortisol concentration in blood plasma samples (ng/mL). normal
Presence or absence of sharks in different locations. Bernoulli







TipLearn why






The number of bees per minute is a count over a fixed time window, so a starting point would be a Poisson distribution.
The number of germinated seeds sounds like a count, but beware: there is a hard upper limit (\(20\) seeds planted). Hence, it is better to consider this the number of successes out of \(20\) trials (a ratio), which can be modeled with a binomial distribution.
Concentration is a continuous outcome, so a starting point could be an ordinary linear model (normal distribution). If cortisol concentrations turn out to be highly skewed, we could try transformation (e.g., modeling \(\log_{10}(\mathrm{concentration})\) instead), or using a distribution that can be right-skewed, like the gamma distribution.
If we don’t count sharks, but simply note their presence/absence, this is a binary outcome. This can be modeled with a binomial distribution with a single trial. This is also called a Bernoulli distribution.








Question 3Answer


Which statements are correct?

Overdispersion leads to poor estimates of the intercept and slope.
Correlation among observations can cause both over- and underdispersion.
Overdispersion can be resolved by changing link functions.
Counts are always (conditionally) Poisson distributed.
A negative binomial distribution can be used to model count data.
Ordinary linear models cannot be overdispersed.







NoteHint





All of these are covered in the  fourth video on GLM.





Which statements are correct?

Overdispersion leads to poor estimates of the intercept and slope.
Correlation among observations can cause both over- and underdispersion.
Overdispersion can be resolved by changing link functions.
Counts are always (conditionally) Poisson distributed.
A negative binomial distribution can be used to model count data.
Ordinary linear models cannot be overdispersed.







TipLearn why






Overdispersion means that at any predicted value of the outcome, there is more spread in observed values than you would expect. This means 1 is incorrect, because the issue is not the estimates but their uncertainty (standard errors).
Positive correlation leads to overdispersion, whereas negative correlation leads to underdispersion, as shown in the  video on overdispersion. Hence, 2 is correct.
Changing a link function changes the estimated relationship (although usually the effect is small). For the same reason as 1 then, 3 is incorrect, as excess spread is not addressed this way.
A Poisson distribution does arise in theory if counts are independent and occurring at a fixed rate. However, in real life, these are rarely realistic assumptions and at best, they hold approximately. Hence, 4 is incorrect.
Despite the name, negative binomial is an alternative to the Poisson (not binomial) distribution that is commonly used to address overdispersion. Hence, 5 is correct.
Overdispersion happens because the Poisson and binomial distribution only have a single free parameter (\(\lambda\) and \(p\), respectively). In ordinary linear models, there is a separate parameter for the variance (\(\sigma^2\)), so it is not possible to have overdispersion. Hence, 6 is correct. Variance is not always constant in ordinary linear models, but that is a separate issue.
