title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Linear regression with any number of explanatory variables.

Multiple linear regression allows you to simultaneously take into account the effect of multiple explanatory variables.


Why not just several one-on-one analyses?

One-on-one measures of association, like a correlation coefficient, are easy to compute and hence often used to explore relationships. However, these fail to reflect the complexity of real-life phenomena. Cancer is not caused by a single mutation; speciation not triggered by a single trait change.
Attempting to understand a complex system by inspecting one-on-one relationships between variables is called correlation analysis. Correlation analysis has been criticized in many biological fields, including clinical science [1]–[3], ecology [4] and evolutionary biology [5]. Key phenomena invalidating one-on-one analyses are explained below.

Omitted Variable BiasSimpson’s Paradox


Estimating the effect of one variable without accounting for the effect of others can lead to a biased result.








Figure 1: True relationship (left) and biased estimate (right) if \(\boldsymbol{O}\) is not included in the model. Arrows are effects on the outcome (\(\boldsymbol{Y}\)); the line means that \(\boldsymbol{O}\) and \(\boldsymbol{X}\) are related.











CautionExample





In a study on asbestos exposure, smoking may be more common among individuals exposed to asbestos. This would lead to an overestimated effect of asbestos, if smoking behavior is not adjusted for. Large systematic reviews on asbestos exposure therefore almost always adjust for smoking [6]–[8].






An example of confounding. Trends can appear, disappear and even completely change direction when including another variable in the model.








Figure 2: Observed trend excluding (left) and including (right) a grouping variable (\(x_2\)).











CautionExample





A study on kidney stones compared two methods for removal: open surgery and percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PN) [9]. Surprisingly, the less invasive PN method displayed a higher success rate than open surgery.
As shown in Table 1, this is an example of Simpson’s paradox: Separating by kidney stone size reveals that open surgery outperforms PN for both situations individually, but not when comparing the totals.



Table 1: Success rates of kidney stone removal methods by size.

How is this contradiction possible? Open surgery is used more often in severe cases (i.e., larger stones), which have a lower success rate. This lowers the total success rate below that of PN. Failing to account for this second variable (size) leads to the wrong conclusion that open surgery performs worse.






Contrary to one-on-one analyses, multiple regression can simultaneously take into account the effect of multiple contributing factors. This allows you to see what the effect of one variable is given the effect of all other included variables, which avoids the phenomena described above, provided those variables were measured and included.
Which variables to include, and which to leave out, is covered in Model Selection.

This part is split into four chapters:

Categorical Variables (dummy variables)
Additive Effects (more than one explanatory variable)
Interaction (when the effect of one variable depends on another)
Model Selection (how the goal of the analysis decides how to choose the model)

To get started, read the summary on categorical variables.
The first three chapters end with the regression tables app to test your knowledge and the ultimate goal: A full analysis for you to do in RStudio.






TipWhat level of detail do I need for the exam?





If you are using this book in the context of one of my courses, please note the following:

On the exam, you interpret these models from their regression table. Focus on what each row means.
Some examples use 3D plots to visually explain what the coefficients mean. However, you do not need to read or draw such plots yourself. In practice, 3D plots are rarely used, because they are hard to judge objectively. Researchers use other tools instead, such as marginal effects plots and interaction plots.

Two groupsAny number of groups











Figure 3.1: One explanatory variable (diet) consisting of 2 categories and the estimated mean of each group.(Mass of 30 fish on two diets.)






Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
  \eta &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x \\ \tag{1}\label{dummy2}\\
  x &=\begin{cases}1 \quad \text{if B}\\ 0 \quad \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\end{align}\]


Code:


RPython



model <- lm(y ~ group, data)




import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
model = smf.ols("y ~ group", data).fit()












NoteSymbols & definitions






\(\eta\) — linear predictor

The linear combination of the explanatory variables and their coefficients.For ordinary linear models, this is just the predicted value of the outcome (\(y\)).

\(x\) — explanatory variable (dummy)

A dummy variable can only take on one of two values, \(0\) or \(1\). It works like a switch: In group B, it is on (\(x = 1\)) and adds \(\beta_1\) to \(\eta\). For all other groups (in this case only A), it is off (\(x = 0\)).

\(\beta_0\) — intercept

Value of the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x\) is zero.Here, \(x\) is zero in group A (the reference group), so this is simply \(\eta\) in group A.

\(\beta_1\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x\) increases by one.Here, \(x\) can only increase from \(0\) (group A) to \(1\) (group B), so this is the difference in \(\eta\) between group B and group A.











TipExplanation





Linear models work with numbers, but a categorical variable consists of labels (e.g., group A and group B). A dummy variable translates those labels into a \(0\) or a \(1\), so that they can be used in the formula. You do not have to create it yourself: R and Python do this automatically for a categorical variable. The coefficient \(\beta_1\) in this case is the difference between the groups:








Figure 3.2: The intercept (\(\beta_0\)) is \(\eta\), when \(x = 0\) (group A). The slope (\(\beta_1\)) is the change in \(\eta\), when \(x\) increases by \(1\) (from group A to group B).

The group in which the dummy variable is zero is called the reference group. By default, this is the first group in alphabetical order. With two groups, choosing the other group as the reference does not change the model: The intercept becomes the mean of group B, and the slope keeps its size, but changes sign.









CautionExample





Fitted to the data of Figure 3.1, the model gives the following estimates:

The estimated mean of the reference group (A) is given by (Intercept) (5.1). For group B, we have to add groupB and the mean becomes 7.06. Apparently, this difference is significant (\(p = 3.92 \times 10^{-6}\)).


Comparison with a classical \(t\)-test

The \(p\)-value of the slope in the regression table tests whether the difference between the groups is zero. This is the same test as a two-sample \(t\)-test with equal variances: Both give the same \(t\)-value and the same \(p\)-value:

Code:


RPython

import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

NoteSymbols & definitions






\(\eta\) — linear predictor

The linear combination of the explanatory variables and their coefficients.For ordinary linear models, this is just the predicted value of the outcome (\(y\)).

\(x_1, x_2\) — explanatory variables (dummy variables)

Translate the groups into numbers that can be used in the formula, one for each group except the reference group (A). Each works like a switch: \(x_1\) is on in group B and adds \(\beta_1\) to \(\eta\); \(x_2\) is on in group C and adds \(\beta_2\); in group A, both are off.

\(\beta_0\) — intercept

Value of the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are zero.Here, both are zero in group A (the reference group), so this is \(\eta\) in group A.

\(\beta_1\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_1\) increases by one.Here, \(x_1\) can only increase from \(0\) (group A) to \(1\) (group B), so this is the difference in \(\eta\) between group B and group A.

\(\beta_2\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_2\) increases by one.Here, \(x_2\) can only increase from \(0\) (group A) to \(1\) (group C), so this is the difference in \(\eta\) between group C and group A.











TipExplanation





With more than two groups, a single dummy variable is no longer enough. Every group except the reference group gets its own dummy variable, and with it, its own difference from the reference group:








Figure 3.4: The intercept (\(\beta_0\)) is \(\eta\) in group A, where both dummy variables are zero. The slopes (\(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\)) are the differences of group B and group C with group A.

Careful, the \(p\)-values of groupB and groupC only tell you whether these groups differ from the reference group. They do not tell you whether B differs from C, nor whether there are any differences between the groups at all.


How to change the reference group

By default, the reference group is the first group in alphabetical order. With more than two groups, the choice matters: It determines which differences the regression table shows. The model itself does not change, so neither do the estimated means, nor the omnibus test.

data$group <- relevel(factor(data$group), ref = "C")

model = smf.ols("y ~ C(group, Treatment(reference='C'))", data).fit()







How to compare all groups at once

3.2 Quiz

Question 1Answer


A colleague compares the height of 45 trees between three sites. In the data, the sites are coded as 1, 2 and 3. This is the resulting regression table:


              Estimate Std. Error    t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 13.5266712  0.7668764 17.6386589 2.643897e-21
site         0.1358843  0.3549948  0.3827782 7.037699e-01


site is not significant (\(p = 0.704\)), so the colleague concludes tree height does not differ significantly between sites. What went wrong? (choose one)
A. Site 1 is missing from the table, so its trees were left out of the analysis
B. site was treated as a continuous variable, so the model assumes that the mean height changes by the same amount from site 1 to site 2 as from site 2 to site 3
C. Three sites need three dummy variables, but the model has only one
D. 15 trees per site are too few to detect a difference in height






NoteHint





Count the rows of the table. How many dummy variables do three groups need?





A colleague compares the height of 45 trees between three sites. In the data, the sites are coded as 1, 2 and 3. This is the resulting regression table:


              Estimate Std. Error    t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 13.5266712  0.7668764 17.6386589 2.643897e-21
site         0.1358843  0.3549948  0.3827782 7.037699e-01


site is not significant (\(p = 0.704\)), so the colleague concludes tree height does not differ significantly between sites. What went wrong? (choose one)
A. Site 1 is missing from the table, so its trees were left out of the analysis
B. site was treated as a continuous variable, so the model assumes that the mean height changes by the same amount from site 1 to site 2 as from site 2 to site 3
C. Three sites need three dummy variables, but the model has only one
D. 15 trees per site are too few to detect a difference in height






TipLearn why





A. All 45 trees are in the model. Site 1 has no row because there are no dummy variables at all: site is a slope, and the intercept is the mean height at a ‘site 0’ that does not exist.
B. Because the sites are coded as numbers, the model treats site as a continuous variable: Every step from one site to the next changes the mean height by the same amount (0.14 m). The site numbers are only labels, so this makes no sense. The mean heights at the three sites are 12.7, 15.8, 12.9 m: up and back down, which a single slope cannot describe.
C. Three groups need two dummy variables, not three: The first group is the reference group, in the intercept. With dummy variables, the table would have two rows, site2 and site3.
D. There are enough trees. With site as a categorical variable, the same 45 trees show that site 2 differs from site 1 (\(p = 6.60 \times 10^{-8}\)).
To fix this, tell R or Python that site is categorical: factor(site) in R, or C(site) in Python.







Question 2Answer


Below is the regression table of the Example under Any number of groups: the mass of fish on three diets.


             Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 5.2573856  0.2948527 17.830551 3.319493e-21
groupB      1.9425723  0.4169846  4.658618 3.199244e-05
groupC      0.5016196  0.4169846  1.202969 2.357259e-01


Which of the following does this table show? (true or false for each)
1. Diet B differs significantly from diet A
2. Diets B and C differ significantly
3. Diets A and C do not differ
4. The table tests whether diet has an overall effect on mass






NoteHint





Each row compares one group with the reference group. See also the note below the table in the Example.





Below is the regression table of the Example under Any number of groups: the mass of fish on three diets.


             Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 5.2573856  0.2948527 17.830551 3.319493e-21
groupB      1.9425723  0.4169846  4.658618 3.199244e-05
groupC      0.5016196  0.4169846  1.202969 2.357259e-01


Which of the following does this table show? (true or false for each)
1. Diet B differs significantly from diet A — True
2. Diets B and C differ significantly — False
3. Diets A and C do not differ — False
4. The table tests whether diet has an overall effect on mass — False






TipLearn why





1. The row groupB is the difference between diet B and the reference group (A), and its \(p\)-value is below \(0.05\).
2. No row compares B with C: Both rows are differences from the reference group (A). That groupB is significant and groupC is not does not mean that B and C differ significantly. This takes pairwise comparisons, or another reference group. The pairwise comparisons in the Example do find a difference, but this table cannot show it.
3. The row groupC is not significant, but absence of evidence is not proof of absence (see the common misconceptions about \(p\)-values).
4. The table tests each group against the reference group, not all groups at once. That takes an omnibus test, as shown in the Example.

Continuous & groupsGroups & groupsContinuous & continuous











Figure 4.1: One continuous and one categorical explanatory variable and the estimated line of each group.(Exercise and systolic blood pressure of 40 patients with hypertension on two drugs.)






Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
  \eta &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_1 + \beta_2 \cdot x_2 \\ \tag{1}\label{additiveslope}\\
  x_2 &=\begin{cases}1 \quad \text{if B}\\ 0 \quad \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\end{align}\]


Code:


RPython



model <- lm(y ~ x + group, data)




import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
model = smf.ols("y ~ x + group", data).fit()












NoteSymbols & definitions






\(\eta\) — linear predictor

The linear combination of the explanatory variables and their coefficients.For ordinary linear models, this is just the predicted value of the outcome (\(y\)).

\(x_1\) — explanatory variable (continuous)

The variable the outcome is regressed on.

\(x_2\) — explanatory variable (dummy)

Translates the groups into a number that can be used in the formula. It works like a switch: In group B, it is on (\(x_2 = 1\)) and adds \(\beta_2\) to \(\eta\); in group A (the reference group), it is off (\(x_2 = 0\)).

\(\beta_0\) — intercept

Value of the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are zero.Here, \(x_2\) is zero in group A (the reference group), so this is \(\eta\) in group A at \(x_1 = 0\).

\(\beta_1\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_1\) increases by one, while \(x_2\) stays the same.Here, this change is the same in group A and group B: The lines of both groups are parallel.

\(\beta_2\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_2\) increases by one, while \(x_1\) stays the same.Here, \(x_2\) can only increase from \(0\) (group A) to \(1\) (group B), so this is the difference in \(\eta\) between group B and group A, at any value of \(x_1\): The distance between the parallel lines.











TipExplanation





With a continuous variable and a dummy variable in the same model, each group gets its own line. Without interaction, both groups share a single slope, so the lines are parallel. The coefficient \(\beta_2\) is the distance between the lines:








Figure 4.2: The intercept (\(\beta_0\)) is \(\eta\) in group A, when \(x_1 = 0\). The slope \(\beta_1\) is the same in both groups, and \(\beta_2\) is the distance between the parallel lines.





The two lines of A and B are then defined as follows:

Purpose of the coefficients.



Intercept
Slope

\(\beta_1\)


B
\(\beta_0 + \beta_2\)
\(\beta_1\)



A model with a single slope for both groups is called a main effects model. It assumes the fitted lines are parallel. If the slopes differ, see the next chapter, interaction.

print(pd.DataFrame({"estimate": tt.effect, "SE": tt.sd.ravel(), "t": t, "p (Tukey)": p},

Figure 4.4: Two categorical variables and the estimated mean of each combination.(Dry mass of 40 plants of two varieties, with and without fertilizer treatment.)






Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
  \eta &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_1 + \beta_2 \cdot x_2 \\ \tag{2}\label{additivedummy}\\
  x_1 &=\begin{cases}1 \quad \text{if B}\\ 0 \quad \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\\
  x_2 &= \begin{cases}1 \quad \text{if treated}\\ 0 \quad \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\end{align}\]


Code:


RPython



model <- lm(y ~ group + treatment, data)




import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
model = smf.ols("y ~ group + treatment", data).fit()












NoteSymbols & definitions






\(\eta\) — linear predictor

The linear combination of the explanatory variables and their coefficients.For ordinary linear models, this is just the predicted value of the outcome (\(y\)).

\(x_1, x_2\) — explanatory variables (dummy variables)

Translate both categorical variables into numbers that can be used in the formula. Each works like a switch: \(x_1\) is on in group B and adds \(\beta_1\) to \(\eta\); \(x_2\) is on for treated observations and adds \(\beta_2\); for untreated observations in group A, both are off.

\(\beta_0\) — intercept

Value of the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are zero.Here, both are zero for untreated observations in group A (the reference groups), so this is \(\eta\) in untreated group A.

\(\beta_1\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_1\) increases by one, while \(x_2\) stays the same.Here, \(x_1\) can only increase from \(0\) (group A) to \(1\) (group B), so this is the difference in \(\eta\) between group B and group A, the same with and without treatment.

\(\beta_2\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_2\) increases by one, while \(x_1\) stays the same.Here, \(x_2\) can only increase from \(0\) (untreated) to \(1\) (treated), so this is the difference in \(\eta\) between treated and untreated, the same in group A and group B.











TipExplanation





With two categorical variables in the same model, both get their own dummy variable. Without interaction, their effects simply add up: The difference between treated and untreated (\(\beta_2\)) is the same in group A and group B:








Figure 4.5: The intercept (\(\beta_0\)) is \(\eta\) in untreated group A. The slope \(\beta_1\) is the difference between group B and group A, and \(\beta_2\) is the difference between treated and untreated.

A model in which the difference between treated and untreated is the same in both groups is called a main effects model. If that difference varies between groups, see the next chapter, interaction.

The linear combination of the explanatory variables and their coefficients.For ordinary linear models, this is just the predicted value of the outcome (\(y\)).

With two continuous variables in the same model, each gets its own slope. Without interaction, the slope of one variable is the same at any value of the other. Instead of a line, the model is now a flat plane:

title: 4  Additive Effects
text:
4.2 Quiz

Question 1Answer


A researcher compares the blood pressure of patients on two drugs and finds no significant difference (\(p = 0.31\)). After adding the hours of exercise per week to the model, the estimated difference between the drugs is almost the same, but it is now significant (\(p = 0.002\)). What is the most likely explanation? (choose one)
A. Exercise was a confounder, so the first estimate was biased
B. Exercise explains much of the variation in blood pressure, so the difference between the drugs is estimated more precisely
C. Adding an explanatory variable always lowers the \(p\)-values of the others
D. The drugs differ more in patients who exercise more






NoteHint





The estimate hardly changed. What else does a test statistic depend on?





A researcher compares the blood pressure of patients on two drugs and finds no significant difference (\(p = 0.31\)). After adding the hours of exercise per week to the model, the estimated difference between the drugs is almost the same, but it is now significant (\(p = 0.002\)). What is the most likely explanation? (choose one)
A. Exercise was a confounder, so the first estimate was biased
B. Exercise explains much of the variation in blood pressure, so the difference between the drugs is estimated more precisely
C. Adding an explanatory variable always lowers the \(p\)-values of the others
D. The drugs differ more in patients who exercise more






TipLearn why





A. A confounder changes the estimate itself (see omitted variable bias). Here, the estimated difference stayed almost the same.
B. The \(t\)-value is the estimate divided by its standard error. Without exercise in the model, the variation in blood pressure that is due to exercise ends up in the residual variance, which makes the standard error large. With exercise in the model, the residual variance is smaller, and so is the standard error. The tutorial on a linear model shows an example.
C. It can also raise them, for example when the added variable is strongly related to another explanatory variable. And adding variables until a result is significant is not a fixed plan (see limitations of hypothesis testing).
D. That would be an interaction. This model has none: It assumes the difference between the drugs is the same at every amount of exercise.







Question 2Answer


A binomial GLM without interaction models the probability of death of rats as a function of the concentration of a toxic gas (\(x_1\)) and sex (\(x_2\)), as in the tutorial on a binomial GLM. Which statement is correct? (choose one)
A. The difference in the probability of death between male and female rats is the same at every concentration
B. The difference in the log-odds of death between male and female rats is the same at every concentration
C. Plotted as probabilities, the curves of male and female rats are parallel
D. If the plotted curves are not parallel, the model must contain an interaction






NoteHint





On which scale is a GLM linear? See the formula of a binomial GLM.





A binomial GLM without interaction models the probability of death of rats as a function of the concentration of a toxic gas (\(x_1\)) and sex (\(x_2\)), as in the tutorial on a binomial GLM. Which statement is correct? (choose one)
A. The difference in the probability of death between male and female rats is the same at every concentration
B. The difference in the log-odds of death between male and female rats is the same at every concentration
C. Plotted as probabilities, the curves of male and female rats are parallel
D. If the plotted curves are not parallel, the model must contain an interaction






TipLearn why





A. The effects add up on the scale of the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), which for a binomial GLM is the log-odds. Translated back to probabilities, the difference is not constant: In the tutorial, it is \(4.3\) percentage points at \(0\) ppm, but \(28.3\) at \(20\) ppm.
B. This is what ‘without interaction’ means in a GLM: \(\beta_2\) is added to \(\eta\) at any value of \(x_1\).
C. The lines are parallel on the scale of \(\eta\) only. As probabilities, both curves are squeezed between \(0\) and \(1\), so the distance between them changes.
D. Curves that are not parallel on the scale of the outcome are what a GLM without interaction looks like. Interaction means that the lines are not parallel on the scale of \(\eta\).

title: 5  Interaction
text:
Slope depends on groupDifference depends on groupSlope depends on other slope











Figure 5.1: Interaction between a continuous and categorical explanatory variable. The effect of age differs, depending on the diet. The resulting lines are not parallel. (Age and mass of 40 fish on two diets.)






Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
  \eta &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_1 + \beta_2 \cdot x_2 + \beta_3 \cdot x_1 \cdot x_2 \\ \tag{1}\label{interactionslope}\\
  x_2 &=\begin{cases}1 \quad \text{if B}\\ 0 \quad \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\end{align}\]


Code:


RPython



model <- lm(y ~ x * group, data)

Note that x * group is shorthand notation for x + group + x:group.



import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
model = smf.ols("y ~ x * group", data).fit()

Note that x * group is shorthand notation for x + group + x:group.











NoteSymbols & definitions






\(\eta\) — linear predictor

The linear combination of the explanatory variables and their coefficients.For ordinary linear models, this is just the predicted value of the outcome (\(y\)).

\(x_1\) — explanatory variable (continuous)

The variable the outcome is regressed on.

\(x_2\) — explanatory variable (dummy)

Translates the groups into a number that can be used in the formula. It works like a switch: In group B, it is on (\(x_2 = 1\)) and adds \(\beta_2\) and \(\beta_3 \cdot x_1\) to \(\eta\); in group A (the reference group), it is off (\(x_2 = 0\)).

\(x_1 \cdot x_2\) — interaction term

Allows the effect of one variable to differ depending on the value of the other.In group B, it adds an additional \(\beta_3\) to the slope. In group A, \(x_2 = 0\), so it adds nothing.

\(\beta_0\) — intercept

Value of the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are zero.Here, \(x_2\) is zero in group A (the reference group), so this is \(\eta\) in group A at \(x_1 = 0\).

\(\beta_1\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_1\) increases by one.In the example, this is the slope of age for diet A (the reference group).

\(\beta_2\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_2\) increases by one.In the example, this is the difference in mean mass between diet B and diet A at age \(0\): The difference in intercept.

\(\beta_3\) — slope (interaction)

Change in the slope of \(x_1\), when \(x_2\) increases by one.Here, \(x_2\) can only increase from \(0\) (group A) to \(1\) (group B), so this is the difference in the slope of \(x_1\) between group B and group A.











TipExplanation





In the previous chapter, both groups shared a single slope, forcing the lines to be parallel. An interaction removes that restriction: Each group gets its own slope. The coefficient \(\beta_3\) in this case is the difference in slope for group B:








Figure 5.2: Visual interpretation of interaction when \(x_1\) is continuous and \(x_2\) a dummy variable.





The two lines of A and B are then defined as follows:

Purpose of the coefficients.



Intercept
Slope




A
\(\beta_0\)
\(\beta_1\)


B
\(\beta_0 + \beta_2\)
\(\beta_1 + \beta_3\)



In a GLM, these are the intercept and slope of the linear predictor (\(\eta\)): The difference in slope (\(\beta_3\)) is on the scale of the link function, not on the scale of the outcome.

Be careful: In a model with interaction, you cannot interpret the coefficients separately: The estimated slope of x (0.94) is the slope of the reference group (A). For group B, we have to add x:groupB and the slope becomes 2.08. Apparently, this difference is significant (\(p = 1.96 \times 10^{-7}\)).


What if there are more than two groups?









Figure 5.3: The data of Figure 5.1 with a third diet, and the estimated line of each diet.(Age and mass of 60 fish on three diets.)





With more than two groups, every group except the reference group gets its own offset from the intercept and its own difference from the reference slope:

Careful, these \(p\)-values only tell you whether the slopes differ from the reference group.

To test the overall interaction, use an omnibus test instead. This gives a single \(p\)-value for the question: “Is there any difference among slopes?”

Apparently, the interaction is significant (\(p = 8.99 \times 10^{-7}\)). Note that if it were not, the other rows of the regression table still only apply to the reference group (x) and to \(x_1 = 0\) (groupB, groupC): Do not use a model with interaction to draw conclusions about x or group on their own. A non-significant interaction is no reason to refit a model without it. Do so only if the interaction is negligible, that is, if its confidence interval lies entirely within differences that are not biologically relevant (see Model Selection).

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import studentized_range

tt = model.t_test(["x:group[T.B] = 0", "x:group[T.C] = 0", "x:group[T.C] - x:group[T.B] = 0"])
t = tt.tvalue.ravel()
p = studentized_range.sf(np.abs(t) * np.sqrt(2), 3, model.df_resid)
print(pd.DataFrame({"estimate": tt.effect, "SE": tt.sd.ravel(), "t": t, "p (Tukey)": p},
                   index=["B - A", "C - A", "C - B"]))

Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
  \eta &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_1 + \beta_2 \cdot x_2 + \beta_3 \cdot x_1 \cdot x_2 \\ \tag{2}\label{interactiondummy}\\
  x_1 &=\begin{cases}1 \quad \text{if B}\\ 0 \quad \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \\
  x_2 &= \begin{cases}1 \quad \text{if treated}\\ 0 \quad \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\end{align}\]


Code:


RPython



model <- lm(y ~ group * treatment, data)




import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

NoteSymbols & definitions






\(\eta\) — linear predictor

The linear combination of the explanatory variables and their coefficients.For ordinary linear models, this is just the predicted value of the outcome (\(y\)).

\(x_1, x_2\) — explanatory variables (dummy variables)

Translate both categorical variables into numbers that can be used in the formula. Each works like a switch: \(x_1\) is on in group B and adds \(\beta_1\) to \(\eta\); \(x_2\) is on for treated observations and adds \(\beta_2\); for untreated observations in group A, both are off.

\(x_1 \cdot x_2\) — interaction term

Allows the effect of one variable to differ depending on the value of the other. It works like a switch too: It is only on for treated observations in group B, and then adds \(\beta_3\) to \(\eta\).

\(\beta_0\) — intercept

Value of the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are zero.Here, both are zero for untreated observations in group A (the reference groups), so this is \(\eta\) in untreated group A.

\(\beta_1\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_1\) increases by one.In the example, this is the difference in mean dry mass between variety B and variety A, for untreated plants.

\(\beta_2\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_2\) increases by one.In the example, this is the difference in mean dry mass between treated and untreated plants, for variety A.

\(\beta_3\) — slope (interaction)

Change in the slope of \(x_1\), when \(x_2\) increases by one.Here, this is how much the difference between group B and group A differs between treated and untreated. Or equivalently, how much the difference between treated and untreated differs between group B and group A.











TipExplanation





In the previous chapter, the difference between treated and untreated was the same in both groups. An interaction removes that restriction: Each group gets its own difference. The coefficient \(\beta_3\) in this case is the difference in differences for group B:








Figure 5.5: The difference between group B and group A is \(\beta_1\) in untreated, and \(\beta_1 + \beta_3\) in treated. The difference between treated and untreated in group A is \(\beta_2\).

NoteSymbols & definitions






\(\eta\) — linear predictor

The linear combination of the explanatory variables and their coefficients.For ordinary linear models, this is just the predicted value of the outcome (\(y\)).

\(x_1, x_2\) — explanatory variables (continuous)

The variables the outcome is regressed on.

\(x_1 \cdot x_2\) — interaction term

Allows the effect of one variable to differ depending on the value of the other.At \(x_2 = 0\), it adds nothing to the slope of \(x_1\); at \(x_2 = 1\), it adds \(\beta_3\); at \(x_2 = 2\), it adds \(2 \cdot \beta_3\); and so on.

\(\beta_0\) — intercept

Value of the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are zero.

\(\beta_1\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_1\) increases by one.In the example, this is the slope of nitrogen for plants that received no phosphorus.

\(\beta_2\) — slope

Change in the linear predictor (\(\eta\)), when \(x_2\) increases by one.In the example, this is the slope of phosphorus for plants that received no nitrogen.

\(\beta_3\) — slope (interaction)

Change in the slope of \(x_1\), when \(x_2\) increases by one.Or equivalently, the change in the slope of \(x_2\), when \(x_1\) increases by one.











TipExplanation





In the previous chapter, the slope of \(x_1\) was the same at any value of \(x_2\), which made the model a flat plane. An interaction removes that restriction: The plane is curved. The coefficient \(\beta_3\) in this case is the change in the slope of \(x_1\), when \(x_2\) increases by one:








Figure 5.7: Visual interpretation of interaction when \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are both continuous. The slope of \(x_1\) is \(\beta_1\) at \(x_2 = 0\) and \(\beta_1 + \beta_3\) at \(x_2 = 1\): Higher with positive interaction (left, the shape of Figure 5.6), lower with negative interaction (right).





Grouping the terms shows that \(x_2\) changes both the intercept and the slope of \(x_1\):
\[\eta = \underbrace{(\beta_0 + \beta_2 \cdot x_2)}_{\text{intercept}} + \underbrace{(\beta_1 + \beta_3 \cdot x_2)}_{\text{slope}} \cdot x_1\]

text:
6.1 Type of Research Question
How to choose the right model for the research question.
So far, we used regression models to estimate the direction, size and significance of effects. This is called inference, and it is one of three ways in which a model can be used [1], [2]. Valid inference requires the model to be chosen before seeing the outcome. Yet, many textbooks, papers and even statistics courses teach choosing the ‘better’ looking model with measures like AIC. How problematic that is depends on the type of research question.
Research questions in empirical1 sciences can be divided into three types:
A study can have several goals. For example, in clinical science, it is not uncommon to have a primary outcome with a planned, preregistered analysis, and subgroup analyses with looser rules, because these are considered exploratory. The most important takeaways:
crumbs: Multiple Linear Regression

title: 6  Model Selection
text:
1 Empirical sciences collect evidence primarily through observations. A counterexample is mathematics, where proofs are derived based on axiomatic truths.
InferenceExplorationPrediction



Estimating the size and direction of an effect; testing pre-specified hypotheses.

Example questions:


Does a compound affect blood pressure?
Which diet is most effective, and by how much?
Does a medicine work differently in men and women? (example of an interaction)


Model selection:

To the extent possible, the primary outcome, model and any hypotheses should be chosen in advance, based on expert knowledge. Some fields even require preregistration.


✓ Choosing a flexible model from the start (e.g., negative binomial instead of Poisson; a spline instead of a linear effect), or making it more flexible when diagnostics reveal a problem you did not foresee, such as a curved relationship.
✓ Reducing dimensions without using the outcome, for example with PCA on the explanatory variables.
✓ Comparing models when the choice of model is the answer to a planned question.(e.g., a model with and without interaction, or competing hypotheses compared by AIC [3])
✗ Using a simpler or less robust analysis because a check found nothing (e.g., a Poisson model after a non-significant test for overdispersion) [4], [5].
✗ Adding or dropping terms by their \(p\)-values, adjusted \(R^2\), AIC, BIC or another measure of fit (see Section 6.4).



Reporting:

Mention every choice made in analysis, and show whether another reasonable choice would change the conclusion. A convention used in some fields is reporting two models: One with only the variables of interest and one that adds all suspected confounders [6].



Making sense of large datasets; finding patterns for follow-up studies; generating new hypotheses.

Example questions:


How are 20 biomarkers for sepsis related to each other?
What adaptations to drought are typical of plants growing in dunes?
Do some bird species respond more strongly to urban noise than others? (After concluding that birds respond significantly to urban noise)


Model selection:

Any method is acceptable, including choosing variables based on the measures for comparing models later in this chapter. However, some methods are less stable than others. With stepwise selection, which adds or removes one variable at a time, a slightly different sample often leads to a different set of variables, especially when the variables are correlated [7]. Treat selected variables as a ‘plausible set’ at best.

Reporting:

Report everything you tried, and clearly indicate—including in the abstract—that the study is exploratory in nature. The same data cannot be used to generate and test the same hypothesis (i.e., moving the goalpost after kicking the ball).


✓ Presenting the findings as hypotheses for a follow-up study.
✗ Disguising an exploratory study as confirmational.(e.g., “We found a significant effect of A and B, but not of C.”)





Predicting the outcome of new observations.

Example questions:


Which patients should receive treatment?
What is a patient’s risk of a heart attack in the next ten years?
Which coral reefs will bleach during the next marine heatwave?


Model selection:

Predictive modeling uses a holdout set, or cross-validation, to report performance on unseen observations. Model selection is fine for predictive modeling, as long as you include any model selection in the training procedure. Additionally, model selection can itself overfit, because the more models you compare, the more likely the best one partly fits noise in the data used to choose it [8].


✓ Including any variable that improves the predictions, as estimated by cross-validation or approximated by AIC [9].
✗ Using all data (before splitting) to scale or select variables, or any other form of data leakage.
✗ Using the same held-out data to choose the model and report its predictive performance. (That requires a separate test set, or nested cross-validation.)



Reporting:

Report how well the chosen model predicts data that were not used to fit or choose it, using a separate test set or cross-validation. Performance on data used to fit or choose the model will be optimistically biased.
Predictive modeling works quite differently from what this book covers. A great resource is An Introduction to Statistical Learning, free to download in an R and a Python edition. Ch. 5 covers cross-validation and Ch. 6 model selection.





Be transparent: Report every choice in the analysis, including what you tried and did not keep.
Decide the goal before the analysis. It determines which choices are allowed, and a model that is ‘best’ for one goal can be inferior, or even wrong, for another [1].
Data used to choose a model cannot also be used to test it, whether by its \(p\)-values or by its predictive performance.

title: 6  Model Selection
text:
6.2 Choosing the model in advance

Applies to: Inference Exploration Prediction

Standard \(p\)-values and confidence intervals assume that the analysis was fixed before seeing the data [10]. Choices that do not use the outcome are generally safe, as they cannot bias the analysis toward significance. A choice that does use the outcome, such as a change after the diagnostics, should not depend on the estimate of interest [10], [11], and should err on the side of caution. This section explains how to make such choices, and Section 6.4 what happens otherwise.

Which variables to include
Whether a variable belongs in the model depends on how it is related to the explanatory variable of interest (\(\boldsymbol{X}\)) and to the outcome (\(\boldsymbol{Y}\)). A directed acyclic graph (DAG) shows this as a diagram with an arrow from each cause to its effect. (Acyclic means the graph never forms a loop.)

ConfounderMediatorCollider


A confounder affects both the outcome and the variable of interest.








Figure 6.1: Confounding by \(\boldsymbol{C}\): actual relationship (left) and what the model estimates without \(\boldsymbol{C}\) (right).





A confounder \(\boldsymbol{C}\) affects both \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and \(\boldsymbol{Y}\), so the two vary together, even if \(\boldsymbol{X}\) has no effect on \(\boldsymbol{Y}\). A model without \(\boldsymbol{C}\) attributes this to \(\boldsymbol{X}\), so its estimate is biased. Hence, include any confounders in the model.
In interventional studies, randomized treatment allocation averages out confounding effects, but including them can still increase power by explaining part of the spread in the outcome.






CautionExample





Coffee consumption is often linked to lung cancer, but this link is caused by the confounding variable smoking. On average, smokers drink more coffee and are much more likely to develop lung cancer. Large overarching meta-analyses adjusting for smoking typically show that coffee consumption is not a risk factor for lung cancer [12]–[14].

For additional examples of confounding, see: stats.stackexchange.com/q/432866
A left-out confounder can also hide an effect that does exist: stats.stackexchange.com/q/463006







A mediator is a variable through which the variable of interest affects the outcome.








Figure 6.2: Mediation through \(\boldsymbol{M}\): actual relationship (left) and what the model estimates with \(\boldsymbol{M}\) (right).





With a mediator \(\boldsymbol{M}\) in the model, the coefficient of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) measures only the part of its effect that does not run through \(\boldsymbol{M}\) (the direct effect). If the whole effect runs through \(\boldsymbol{M}\), the model finds no effect at all. Hence, leave mediators out of the model. If the purpose of a study is to determine whether an effect is direct or mediated, look up mediation analysis.
In interventional studies, include only variables measured before the treatment started, because the treatment cannot have affected them.






CautionExample





Suppose you want to estimate how much fossil fuel consumption contributes to global warming. CO2 levels are related to global temperature, so it is tempting to include them in the model. However, fossil fuel consumption does not raise the temperature directly. It raises CO2 levels, which in turn raise the temperature.
\[\text{fossil fuel consumption} \to \mathrm{CO}_2 \to \text{average global temperature}\]
In this example, CO2 is a mediator. Including a mediator removes the indirect effect of the variable of interest [15]. With CO2 in the model, the coefficient of fossil fuel consumption is close to zero. That is not wrong, because there is no direct effect, but it also does not answer the question.





A collider is affected by both the variable of interest and the outcome.








Figure 6.3: Collider bias from \(\boldsymbol{K}\): actual relationship (left) and what the model estimates with \(\boldsymbol{K}\) (right).





Because \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and \(\boldsymbol{Y}\) both affect a collider \(\boldsymbol{K}\), observations with the same value of \(\boldsymbol{K}\) that differ in \(\boldsymbol{X}\) tend to differ in \(\boldsymbol{Y}\) as well. With \(\boldsymbol{K}\) in the model, the coefficient of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) describes how \(\boldsymbol{Y}\) differs with \(\boldsymbol{X}\) at the same value of \(\boldsymbol{K}\), so \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and \(\boldsymbol{Y}\) appear related, even if \(\boldsymbol{X}\) has no effect on \(\boldsymbol{Y}\). Hence, leave colliders out of the model.
In interventional studies, include only variables measured before the treatment started, because neither the treatment nor the outcome can have affected them.






CautionExample





Suppose a new antibiotic does not affect how quickly patients with pneumonia recover, but patients who receive it are kept in the hospital one extra day for monitoring. Patients who recover sooner also leave sooner. Among patients who stayed equally long, those on the new antibiotic must then have recovered a day sooner. With length of stay in the model, the antibiotic would seem to shorten recovery, even though it has no effect at all [16].






For your own study, draw a DAG before you collect data: every variable you plan to measure, with an arrow for each effect you expect (see Figure 6.4 for an example). It shows which variables are confounders, mediators or colliders, and it makes your assumptions visible to your readers.


Planned comparisons
Whether to include an interaction does not depend solely on the research question. If subject knowledge suggests that a medicine works differently in men and women, by a clinically relevant amount, then a model without interaction is wrong. Leave it out only if there is no reason to expect it, and do not remove it merely because it is non-significant.
Comparing models is part of the method only if the comparison itself is the planned question, such as whether the effect of the medicine differs between men and women, or which of several competing hypotheses, each written down beforehand as a model, fits best [3]. The comparison then answers that question (see measures for comparing models).


Changing the model after fitting
After fitting, the model may still be changed in two ways:

DiagnosticsRemoving terms



A model chosen in advance can still be wrong in ways the design did not foresee. If the diagnostics reveal a problem, make the model more flexible, for example with an extra term or a transformation for a curved relationship. Report such a change clearly, together with the result of the model as planned. A check that finds nothing, however, is not a valid reason to switch to a simpler model [17] (see Section 6.4).



A non-significant term can still be biologically relevant. Remove a term only if it is negligible, that is, if its 95% confidence interval lies entirely within effects that are not biologically relevant [18]. Which effects are biologically relevant is a subject-matter judgment, made before seeing the data. Confounders should not be removed even then, because a confounder that is strongly related to the variable of interest can bias its estimate, however small its own effect. In a small study, the interval is rarely that narrow. If the interval exceeds the threshold for relevance, do not remove the term from the model. You can conclude that the study could not determine its practical relevance [19].






TipWhat if a suspected interaction turns out to be negligible?





Decide in advance how large an interaction would have to be to matter in practice (\(\delta\)). For example, a difference of less than 5 mmHg in the effect of a medicine between men and women, or a change of less than 1 mmHg in its effect per ten years of age, may not be clinically relevant. If the 95% confidence interval of the interaction lies entirely between \(-\delta\) and \(\delta\), report that the interaction is negligible, and refit the model without it to estimate main effects. If the interval extends beyond \(\delta\), report that the study could not determine whether the interaction matters (but do not remove it from the model).












CautionExample





A study tests whether street lights affect the number of caterpillars in roadside vegetation. Of 40 roadside sites, 20 are chosen at random to get LED street lights, and the other 20 stay dark. Later that season, the caterpillars at each site are counted. Before the lights are installed, two other characteristics of each site are recorded. One is the number of shrub species, since caterpillars feed on shrubs. The other is whether the site borders forest or grassland.
The goal is inferential: Does LED light change the number of caterpillars, and by how much? So we choose the model before the caterpillars are counted. Counts like these are nearly always overdispersed, so we choose a negative binomial GLM instead of a Poisson model. The number of shrub species probably affects the number of caterpillars, so including it makes the estimate of light more precise. Since the shrub species were recorded before the lights were installed, light cannot have affected them. The number of shrub species is therefore neither a mediator nor a collider, and including it does not bias the estimate of light. Habitat could be included for the same reason. Either choice is valid, as long as it is made before seeing the counts. For our example, let’s say we leave habitat out.
We also leave out bat activity during the experiment. Bats hunt the moths that gather around street lights, so light may reduce the number of caterpillars through bat activity, which makes bat activity a possible mediator. Finally, we have no reason to expect light to affect caterpillars differently next to forest than next to grassland, so the model has no interaction.








Figure 6.4: The effects assumed in the street light study. The arrow with the question mark is the effect of interest. Light was assigned at random, so no arrow points to it. Variables in black are in the model; those in grey are left out.





After fitting, we check the model’s diagnostics. Had they revealed a problem (e.g., a curved relationship with the number of shrub species), we would make the model more flexible, and also report the model as planned. Suppose for now that they reveal none. The model then stays as planned. We keep the number of shrub species, whether or not it is significant, and we do not add habitat. The methods and results could read:

The number of caterpillars was analyzed with a negative binomial GLM with light and the number of shrub species, as planned before the data were collected. LED light did not significantly change the number of caterpillars (1.10 times as many as in the dark, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.68, \(p = 0.664\)).

Had we added habitat only after seeing the counts (e.g., because light then became significant), that \(p\)-value would not have been valid (see Section 6.4).

title: 6  Model Selection
text:
6.3 Measures for comparing models

Applies to: Inference Exploration Prediction

For inference, use these measures only to answer a planned comparison.
The measures below weigh how well a model fits, measured by \(-2 \log \mathcal{L}\), against how many parameters it has. \(\mathcal{L}\) is the likelihood: the probability of the observed data under the fitted model. The better a model fits, the lower \(-2 \log \mathcal{L}\).
If one model contains all terms of the other, they can be compared with a likelihood ratio test, a general form of the omnibus test. It tests whether the extra parameters of the larger model are all zero.

Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
\text{LR} &= -2 \log \mathcal{L}_0 - (-2 \log \mathcal{L}_1)
\end{align}\]
where \(\mathcal{L}_0\) is the likelihood of the smaller model (m0 in the code) and \(\mathcal{L}_1\) that of the larger (m1). The \(p\)-value comes from a \(\chi^2\)-distribution with as many degrees of freedom as the larger model has extra parameters. With one extra parameter, \(p < 0.05\) if \(-2 \log \mathcal{L}\) decreases by more than \(3.84\).


Code:


RPython



anova(m0, m1)

anova() performs the likelihood ratio test; for an ordinary linear model, it performs the \(F\)-test, its exact counterpart for the normal distribution.



from scipy import stats
LR = 2 * (m1.llf - m0.llf)
df = m1.df_model - m0.df_model
stats.chi2.sf(LR, df)





Two common measures for model selection are AIC (Akaike information criterion) and BIC (Bayesian information criterion). Lower values are better.

Mathematical formula:

\[\begin{align}
\text{AIC} &= -2 \log \mathcal{L} + 2k \\
\text{BIC} &= -2 \log \mathcal{L} + k \log n
\end{align}\]
where \(k\) is the number of estimated parameters (the coefficients, plus, for example, the dispersion parameter of a negative binomial model), \(n\) the number of observations, and \(\log\) the natural logarithm.
AIC prefers the larger of two models if \(-2 \log \mathcal{L}\) decreases by more than \(2\) per extra parameter, BIC if it decreases by more than \(\log n\). From 8 observations on, BIC is therefore stricter. AIC approximates how well a model predicts new observations, as estimated by leave-one-out cross-validation [9]. BIC is preferred when the goal is parsimony (finding as simple a model as possible that explains well).


Code:


RPython



AIC(m0, m1)
BIC(m0, m1)




print(m0.aic, m1.aic)
print(m0.bic, m1.bic)





m0 and m1 stand for any two models of the same outcome, fitted to the same observations. Unlike the likelihood ratio test, AIC and BIC do not require one model to contain the other.

text:
6.4 What data-driven selection does to \(p\)-values and estimates

Applies to: Inference Exploration Prediction

If the analysis is based on the data,2 the false positive rate is no longer guaranteed to be \(\alpha\) [20]. The effect can be large: A simulation study found that deciding whether and how to include just one explanatory variable, and reporting whichever choice gave a significant result, raised the false positive rate from 5% to 12% [21]. Confidence intervals become too narrow, and the effects that are selected are estimated too far from zero, because an effect is more likely to be selected when the sample exaggerates it [7], [22]. Common ways of choosing the model by the data:
2 As opposed to chosen based on the research question, primary outcome and study design.
Selecting termsSimplifying after a check


Stepwise selection, removing terms that are not significant, is the most common example [7], [22]. Removing a confounder because it is not significant also biases the estimate of the effect you are interested in [23]. Likewise, removing an interaction because it is not significant biases the estimates, even if there is no interaction at all [24].
Statistical measures like AIC do not avoid this problem. For a term with one parameter, selection based on lower AIC is identical to selecting \(p\)-values below \(0.157\). R’s step() function, which adds and removes terms by AIC, therefore performs stepwise selection with \(\alpha \approx 0.157\). BIC and adjusted \(R^2\) are likewise thresholds for the \(p\)-value, each with a different \(\alpha\) [7], [25].


A non-significant diagnostic check is not a good reason to switch to a simpler model. With few observations, diagnostics often miss the very problems they are meant to detect, and choosing the model by such a check inflates the false positive rate [17], [26].



For exploratory research, these biases are acceptable, as long as the report clearly states the type of research question. Present the results as hypotheses for further research. Claiming you have found something significant after selecting the model on the same data is analogous to shooting a ball and moving the goalpost to wherever it lands.






ImportantCommon misconceptions about model selection






“Model selection is harmless if done in moderation.”

Even the selection of a single term can greatly affect the false positive rate.

“Model selection is harmless, as long as the selection is reported.”

Reporting the selection is necessary, but it does not make the \(p\)-values valid, because they are computed as if the model had been chosen in advance. Present them as exploratory, or choose the model before seeing the outcome.

“Model selection finds the best model.”

Goodness-of-fit does not show the role of a variable. If light reduces caterpillars by attracting bats, every measure prefers a model with bat activity measured during the experiment. Yet that variable is a mediator, and including it hides the effect of interest (see Mediator).

“Multiple testing correction can account for model selection.”

That works only if every candidate model gives a valid test of the same hypothesis, which is rarely the case. A Poisson model of overdispersed counts, for instance, gives too many false positives, and halving \(\alpha\) does not fix that [27]. With and without the interaction x1:x2, the coefficient of x1 is not even the same effect. With the interaction, it is the effect of x1 where x2 is zero (see Interaction). Methods that do account for the choice of model exist [28], [29], but they are beyond the scope of this book.

title: 6  Model Selection
text:
6.5 Parameters vs. sample size

Applies to: Inference Exploration Prediction

There is a limit to how many parameters you can estimate with a given amount of data. A rough guideline is 10–20 observations per estimated coefficient for continuous outcomes, and 10–20 events of the minority group per coefficient for binary outcomes [29].
Without more advanced techniques, like regularization, a model that has too many parameters relative to the effective sample size will overfit. It describes the sample well, but generalizes poorly to its population. Conversely, a model that is too simple for the pattern in the data will underfit. Figure 6.5 illustrates both.








Figure 6.5: The same 30 observations, fitted with 2, 3 and 16 coefficients. The straight line misses the curve; the 15th-degree polynomial follows the noise, and would predict new observations poorly.





More parameters lower the bias of the predictions, but raise their variance: how much the predictions would change in another sample. The total error is smallest in between (Figure 6.6). For prediction, cross-validation estimates where that balance lies, and AIC approximates it (see measures for comparing models). For inference, the question determines the model. If the data cannot support it, reduce the number of parameters without using the outcome (see What if I have many potential confounders?).








Figure 6.6: Prediction error against model complexity. With too few parameters, the predictions are biased; with too many, they vary strongly from sample to sample. The total error is smallest in between.





Interactions are more ‘expensive’ to estimate. In a balanced design with two groups for each variable, the standard error of an interaction is twice that of a main effect, so estimating it equally precisely takes four times as many observations.
Explanatory variables that carry largely the same information are called colinear.3 The model can then hardly separate their effects, and their standard errors grow [29]. In the extreme, one variable is the sum of others, such as body weight, which is the sum of fat-free mass and fat mass. The model then cannot estimate all three, and R reports NA for one of them. If confounders are perfectly colinear, one of them can be left out, because the others carry the same information. Otherwise, colinearity among confounders is no reason to remove any of them. It widens only their own confidence intervals, not that of the variable of interest, whereas removing a confounder can bias the estimate of interest. There are better ways than including strongly colinear confounders as they are, such as combining them without using the outcome (see What if I have many potential confounders?).
3 Also collinear, or multicollinear, which all have the same meaning.See: stats.stackexchange.com/q/316213





TipWhat if I have many potential confounders?





As confounders are usually not of interest to the research question, but more of a ‘nuisance’ parameter, you can combine, summarize, or reduce them, as long as you do not use the outcome:

Remember that mediators and colliders do not belong in the model at all. Variables that only affect the outcome are also not needed to avoid bias, so you can leave these out.
Suspected confounders that carry similar information can be summed or otherwise combined. For example, the height and width of a hedge can be multiplied into a single score roughly representing its surface area. Similar categories with very few observations can be merged as well.
Methods like principal component analysis can create a small number of linear combinations of your original confounders. These are harder to interpret, but carry most of the original information, while costing fewer degrees of freedom to estimate.

text:
Quiz

Question 1Answer


A colleague analyzes the number of hospital visits of 15 patients with a Poisson GLM. The dispersion test in the diagnostics is not significant (\(p = 0.21\)), so a Poisson model is kept. Which statement is correct?
A. This is fine, as the test demonstrates there is no overdispersion.
B. A negative binomial model must only be used if the test is significant.
C. A negative binomial model from the start would have been safer.
D. They should report the model with the smallest \(p\)-value for the effect of interest.






NoteHint





What does a non-significant test show? And what does the checklist for inference recommend for counts?





A colleague analyzes the number of hospital visits of 15 patients with a Poisson GLM. The dispersion test in the diagnostics is not significant (\(p = 0.21\)), so a Poisson model is kept. Which statement is correct?
A. This is fine, as the test demonstrates there is no overdispersion.
B. A negative binomial model must only be used if the test is significant.
C. A negative binomial model from the start would have been safer.
D. They should report the model with the smallest \(p\)-value for the effect of interest.






TipLearn why





A. Failure to detect overdispersion does not prove there is none. With only 15 observations, a dispersion test has limited power.
B. Switching only when the test is significant means keeping the Poisson model whenever the test misses overdispersion, which inflates the false positive rate.
C. If you expect overdispersed counts (as is very common for biological processes), a safer choice is using a negative binomial from the start.
D. This increases false positives beyond the chosen level of significance \(\alpha\).







Question 2Answer


A trial compares two medicines in men and women. The interaction between medicine and sex is not significant: The difference in effect between men and women is estimated at \(2.0\) mmHg (95% confidence interval from \(-2.7\) to \(6.7\) mmHg, \(p = 0.40\)). A difference of less than \(5\) mmHg would not matter in practice. What do you do?
A. Remove the interaction, because it is not significant.
B. Remove the interaction, because its estimate is smaller than \(5\) mmHg.
C. Keep the interaction, and conclude that you could not determine whether the effect differs between men and women.
D. Keep the interaction, and report the row of the medicine as its effect in everyone.






NoteHint





When is a term negligible? Compare the confidence interval with the effects that would matter.





A trial compares two medicines in men and women. The interaction between medicine and sex is not significant: The difference in effect between men and women is estimated at \(2.0\) mmHg (95% confidence interval from \(-2.7\) to \(6.7\) mmHg, \(p = 0.40\)). A difference of less than \(5\) mmHg would not matter in practice. What do you do?
A. Remove the interaction, because it is not significant.
B. Remove the interaction, because its estimate is smaller than \(5\) mmHg.
C. Keep the interaction, and conclude that you could not determine whether the effect differs between men and women.
D. Keep the interaction, and report the row of the medicine as its effect in everyone.






TipLearn why





A. A non-significant term is not the same as a negligible one.
B. The estimate alone is not enough. The interval reaches \(6.7\) mmHg, a difference that would matter.
C. The interval includes differences that matter, so the result is inconclusive. To report the average effect of the medicine, estimate it from the model with interaction, using emmeans.
D. In a model with interaction, the row of the medicine is its effect in the reference group only.
